subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PURCHASE OF TURKEYS BY AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS BOARD

speakeroldname: Hon. H. A. Olson (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PURCHASE OF TURKEYS BY AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to announce that the Agricultural Products'Board has been authorized to purchase turkeys for processing, with the canned meat going to the world food program. This action is the first action taken under the previously announced programs designed to offset the impact of the surtax on agricultural products entering the United States. It is estimated that the amount of turkeys purchased will compensate for the market for Canadian turkeys in the United States lost during the period August to December because of the surtax which has further distorted an unbalanced supply and demand situation.
The Agricultural Products Board will be issuing tender calls, specifications and other details shortly.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PURCHASE OF TURKEYS BY AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having regard to the statement just made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) I am aware that the Ontario Turkey Federation made representations to the minister and the board as early as late August or early in September. I have also made strong representations to the minister and the chairman of the Agricultural Products Board in this regard.
We all know that at this time turkey prices are the lowest they have been for 25 years. This has resulted from the fact that when chicken broilers were put on quotas in Quebec many buildings which were easily adaptable to raising turkeys were switched over and there was an increase in turkey production. We now understand that some of the provinces have got together in an endeavour to control their production to some extent to assist in achieving a better price.
The United States surcharge has created a tremendous hardship for turkey producers because the price dropped two cents per pound on its implementation. In addition, the surcharge is causing the loss of many jobs in this country. Canadian hatcheries that produced turkey poults in Canada are finding they cannot sell in the United States because of the increase from two cents to four cents in the duty on turkey poults. Production of turkey poults by Canadian firms in the United States is increasing and Canadian workers are being laid off.
I am sure we are all thankful for the little bit of assistance the minister has announced today. I realize that the producers asked that some 8 million to 10 million pounds of turkeys be purchased for the world food program. The minister has not said how much will be purchased for this purpose, but I do not think the amount will be anything like what was requested, I am sorry to say. I certainly hope that what has been decided will be helpful at the present time and that further action will be taken when necessary. We will expect the government to keep a watchful eye on the situation and take further action in this regard when necessary.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PURCHASE OF TURKEYS BY AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS BOARD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the minister assured the House a while ago that agricultural products affected by the United States surtax would be considered product by product, and I suppose this is another instalment in that procedure. Because I have spoken to producers personally I know that some producers in western Canada are in a very serious situation. The minister's announcement will certainly make them feel somewhat better since he is taking at least this much action to meet the existing situation. Some of them have discussed with me the possibility of finding other markets than the United States and the possibility of research into processing and developing special products. I suppose those who have such ideas will bring them forward to the minister, and I hope he will extend to them whatever co-operation is within his power.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43 I ask the unanimous consent of the House to propose a motion of urgent and pressing necessity.
This matter concerns the decision of the government to support the Albanian resolution at the United Nations. This resolution calls for the recognition of the People's Republic of China and at the same time for the expulsion forthwith of the representatives of Taiwan.
As the government in Taiwan is clearly in de facto control of the Island of Taiwan and adjacent islands, the question arises whether the Albanian resolution is contrary to the United Nations principle of universality of representation. The resolution also creates the precedent of expelling a member from the world body.
I therefore propose to move, seconded by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander):
That the government do forthwith provide an early opportunity before the U.N. vote on the Albanian resolution for full discussion of this important matter in this chamber.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I seek the unanimous consent of the House under Standing Order 43 to place before it a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. It arises out of serious lay-offs made in the last few days by the Polymer Corporation in Sarnia where 250 production and scientific employees have been laid off, some with 25 years of service. The lay-offs were announced by the president of the corporation and services were terminated without notice although employees were given the appropriate pay in lieu of notice. This has caused tremendous hardship for the families concerned and has produced a sense of insecurity not only throughout the Polymer work force but also throughout the community.
Since Polymer is a Crown corporation answerable to this Parliament through the Minister of Supply and Services and since there is great fear that further lay-offs may follow, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the lay-offs which have been imposed by Polymer Corporation and the circumstances leading thereto be referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration for immediate and full inquiry.

I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn), the following motion:

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY   APPARENT BREAKDOWN IN COMMUNICATION BETWEEN GOVERNMENT AND GOVERNMENT OF UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 26 I ask leave to move the adjournment of the House for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration.
This specific and important matter is the apparent breakdown in communication between the government and the government of the United States at a time when confusion regarding economic relations between the two countries must accelerate the rate of unemployment in Canada.
If my motion is acceptable, Mr. Speaker, I will move the adjournment of the House, seconded by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin).

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY   APPARENT BREAKDOWN IN COMMUNICATION BETWEEN GOVERNMENT AND GOVERNMENT OF UNITED STATES
speechtext:
The hon. Leader of the Opposition has filed with the Chair the due notice of his motion to request the adjournment of the House for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration under the provisions of Standing Order 26.
The question which the Chair must determine is whether or not the problem as posed by the Leader of the Opposition meets with the procedural requirements of Standing Order 26.
It is obvious to all hon. members that the general question of communications and relations between the governments of the United States and of Canada is of paramount importance. It is of national and urgent interest. It does not follow necessarily that such a vast and complex prob-

October 12, 1971
Inquiries of the Ministry
lem must be debated today, by an adjournment of our regular proceedings under the terms of Standing Order 26, rather than later this week or next week.
My understanding of Standing Order 26 is that its provisions apply when there is an emergency of a sudden nature which requires an immediate debate in the House. The standing order does not apply when we have before us a situation which is claimed to be developing or evolving over a period of time. Hon. members are well aware that this suggestion has been advanced in the House on a number of occasions in past weeks, and particularly during the lengthy debate which took place in relation to Bill C-262. That condition in itself would tend to indicate that the proposed motion does not satisfy the criteria set out in the standing order.
In view of all circumstances and after reiterating that the Speaker's ruling, in such circumstances, is essentially a procedural one, I must conclude that for today at least the motion cannot be put to the House.

speechtext: The House resumed, from Friday, October 8, consideration of the motion of Mr. Gray (for Mr. Benson) that bill C-259 to amend the Income Tax Act and to make certain provisions and alterations in the statute law related to or consequential upon the amendments to that act, be read the second time and referred to the committee of the whole.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are some points regarding this bill I should like to call to the attention of the House at this stage on second reading. We are discussing an immensely complicated piece of tax legislation. The bill is very complicated, very detailed and very dry. One would have to admit, consequently, that the discussion of this bill is not exactly going to grab the Canadian people.
Nevertheless, the contents of the bill are of tremendous importance to the Canadian people and indeed to the whole future of this country. The most obvious reason is the immediate and long-term effect that this legislation will have upon the pocketbooks of individual Canadians. This is important because it involves the freedom of choice of the individual, his ability to spend his money as he desires, the proportion of his earnings he will have to give to the public treasury for public purposes and the proportion he may be allowed to keep for his own priorities. We of the official opposition have been saying from the start that as a result of the rapidly increasing proportion the government intends to take even from the relatively low wage earners, as their earnings may go up because of inflation or because of an increase in their salary for other reasons, most Canadians would rather quickly find they will be paying more rather than less to the government of Canada.
The sleight of hand trick may well have an effect for a few months or even for a year or two, but the whole thrust of this tax package is to get more money from the low or relatively low income workers. That is what we have been denouncing and continue to denounce. However, beyond the impact on individuals there is another aspect of taxation which affects the whole economy, its capacity for growth, its capacity to adapt to changing conditions in the country and its capacity to adapt to changing conditions in the whole world. The question we must ask ourselves, and ask the government, is what does this proposed tax package really accomplish in terms of the health of the whole Canadian economy. What do these changes do, for example, to help us fight the battle against massive unemployment in Canada. What do they do to help us in the battle against inflation. What do they do to improve or even maintain our trading position in the world, where all the established trading patterns are under attack as they have not been for a long time. The answer must be that this present tax bill is irrelevant to the solution of these problems. That is the best answer one could give.
The most optimistic answer one could give is that this tax bill is irrelevant to the fight against inflation, the fight against unemployment and the fight to enable the Canadi-
October 12, 1971

an economy to adjust to world trading conditions. Indeed, as I say, that is an optimistic point of view to take as I shall indicate in a few moments. Even the government does not pretend that these proposals, if they should be applied at the beginning of next year, would have any real effect on unemployment. That is, they would not in any way reduce unemployment. It is just as well the government does not claim this, because it would be laughed out of court if it were to try to do so. The government does not claim these tax proposals will help in the battle against inflation, that is clear; and once again it is just as well because they could not make any case. As for the present trading position in Canada and Canadian industry, especially with regard to the United States, the relevance of these proposals has not been laid out. It is clear to all of us who have sat in this House and who have lived in Canada for the past number of months that the country is faced with tremendous problems, problems which are immediate and problems which are right here in front of us as well as problems which we see stretching out into the future.
Let us not forget that tax policy, both long and shortterm, inevitably has an enormous impact on our present and future economic performance in Canada.

When the bill was drafted and presented to the House the economic context in which Canada found itself appeared then to be markedly different from the context in which we find ourselves today. It is true we had very heavy unemployment, despite all the predictions of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), but at the time the bill was introduced our exports were doing quite well. It was the unsatisfactory rate of growth in the domestic sector that was generally considered to be causing the unemployment. Indeed, our exports have been expanding because of the expanding economies of our customers.
At the time when the tax bill was introduced I suppose the darkest cloud that was visible on the horizon was the much discussed entry of Great Britain into the Common Market, and the very real and very justified concern as to what this might do to some of our exports. This was the darkest cloud visible on the horizon so far as our exports were concerned. Then, as we know, in mid-August President Nixon announced his new package. We all remember the surtax that was imposed, the visit of two of our ministers to Washington, and the rumours and speculation as to matters between our two countries that the United States wished to see changed. We now know that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) had requested a bill of particulars, so to speak, with regard to the removal of the surtax, but this has not been received. However, there has been a great deal of discussion in the press and elsewhere as to matters for which the U.S. may be pushing in terms of long-term and fundamental changes in the trading relations between our two countries. These suggestions have not only come in the press, indeed they came from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) himself as well as from the Secretary of State for External Affairs.

But if it is- and you know this is your question-if it is, we will have to have a fundamental re-assessment of our whole economy.

Therefore, I suggest that it hardly makes sense to consider a tax bill now which involves a complete new package. It involves a vast change, a reform in the law, if you like, relating to the taxation of the incomes of corporations. It involves, of course, changes in personal income tax schedules and exemptions. It makes a lot of sense to consider these, and I am not suggesting that they should be dropped, but in terms of this vast new structure of taxation of companies, partnerships and business profits generally, I suggest that this whole structure may need substantial revision, even in the eyes of the sponsors of this bill, when the smoke clears and our position vis-a-vis the U.S. in terms of trading relationships becomes clearer. Even those who sponsored this bill last spring may themselves come to feel that this is not the appropriate kind of tax structure for Canada to have in the new circumstances which the Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of Finance have said may be evolving. They have all expressed the hope- and I hope their hope is justified-that any fears they might have would prove groundless.
However, it is hardly sensible for the House to proceed with this tax structure as if nothing at all had happened in view of the quite disquieting statements that the Prime Minister and senior members of his government have made in public. We have the U.S. surtax on many of our exports to the U.S. We have tax changes now before the U.S. congress, including the so-called DISC program. We have the statements of our own ministers that in view of all these things there may be a need for a fundamental revision of our relationship with the U.S. in terms of trade. If this is so, I could say a good deal about the kind of commentary that this deterioration makes on the kind of policy that the government has been pursuing with regard to the United States, but that is not my point today.

I do not rise today to criticize the government in connection with the Canada-U.S. relationship, since there will be another opportunity to do that. My point is that these changes to which the Prime Minister and the ministers have referred may require a quite different approach to business taxation, especially with regard to companies, partnerships and individuals engaged in the exporting business. Premier Davis of Ontario made this point very effectively I think toward the end of last week. It might be said that whatever changes prove to be necessary in any newly evolved international context, whatever that may be, such changes can be made by special legislation in time. If the changes under way are anything as fundamental as the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs have suggested, changes which would require a complete new rethinking of our whole relationship, then the changes in our tax structure to meet this situation may need to be very far reaching. Indeed it might be much more advisable for us to approach this question, and any new stance we wish to adopt by way of incentives, in terms of our general tax reform legislation rather than in terms of special taxation which might attract undue attention and, in the eyes of our competitors, look like a subsidy of some sort.
This bill is enormously complex, especially with regard to small corporations. I do not think anybody will deny for a minute that it will take quite a bit of time for a small company to get used to it. The small businessman will need quite a bit of advice for tax consultants on a continuing basis to learn how to operate satisfactorily in the new milieu that this tax bill would create. In view of its complexity, in view of the difficulties it will create, the added difficulties in the lives of business people at this time, it is not the sort of thing the House should enter upon lightly.
I suggest it does not make very much sense for us to be asked by the government to consider a bill of this complexity at this time if in fact the government is considering other options with regard to Canada's trade stance in the world. If the government feels it is compelled at this time to consider other options with regard to trading policies generally, then it is pretty likely to feel compelled to consider other options with regard to taxation policies, particularly as they effect industries and companies engaged in exports.

Mr. Speaker, I enter the debate at this stage with a speech, which I hope will not be very lengthy, for three reasons which will become evident as I continue.
When the government informs Parliament and the people of Canada that it is engaged in a total reappraisal of its economic relations with the United States which may, as developments occur, become necessary, I think the whole sense of the bill before us becomes rather obscure and difficult to understand. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that there is no way in which such a reappraisal, if it is taking place in the ranks of the government and if it results in some new direction of government policy, can be achieved without affecting the tax structure of Canada.
The tax measures now in this complicated and unreadable bill-I challenge anyone to read this bill in the course of a week and understand at least half of it-really concern in part our economic relations with the United States because they still give emphasis to the resource industries; they still make important tax concessions to the large foreign controlled corporations that yank Canada's wealth out of the ground and ship it elsewhere. That, Mr. Speaker, is one of the basic facts of the present tax bill. As was said during the debate on the budget by members of my party and the hon. member for Duvernay (Mr. Kierans), the general thrust of the proposition of the government is to continue to tax the large corporations and the resource extractive industries lightly and to continue to tax ordinary Canadians heavily. That imbalance, that inequity in the tax system, is directly related to our economic relations with the United States. It is obvious that when one gives corporations that have their headquarters in the United States continuing tax concessions, one invites them to continue controlling our economy and indeed to increase that control.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I say, since it is my wont to speak pretty frankly and strongly, that the government is not being frank with us when it says it is reappraising our economic relations with the United States and when it says that, it is just talking about something that is a theoretical, academic exercise undertaken by the mandarins and their assistants in the various departments as a matter of regular routine rather than as a matter of meaningful reappraisal of our position vis-a-vis the United States. Either that is what is happening or the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) was boasting about something that is not really the case, playing games with words and with the people of Canada. Either that is the case or the government must withdraw the tax bill now before us and look at it again in the light of any reappraisal that is really taking place in government ranks.
That seems perfectly logical to me, Mr. Speaker, because no reassessment of our economic relations with the United States, no program of action and policy following such a reassessment that changes the direction of Canada's economy, that I can conceive of would not involve the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) and his tax

One cannot discuss this bill without dealing with the over-all economic situation that faces Canada. In fact, Mr. Speaker, I feel we are being a little like Alice in Wonderland discussing a huge unreadable and almost unintelligible tax bill at a moment in our economic history when we have had far too high unemployment for the month of August and a threat of massive unemployment in the autumn and winter months. I feel that the government is making this Parliament deal with a subject that is not immediate, which, as far as I am concerned, will have value mainly for the corporations some time hence, when what we ought to be dealing with is the immediate concern of unemployment in Canada and the dreadful-I repeat, Mr. Speaker,-the dreadful situation that the workers of Canada are likely to find themselves in during the next two or three months and for some months to follow. We are told all the time by the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that the government is in the process of working up a program to create jobs this winter and then, there is this delay. Mr. Speaker, I say to the government and the Minister of Finance who is here, that I cannot understand the reasons for that delay. I cannot see anything ahead but great trouble and hardship as a result of that delay.
In answer to a question which I put to him the other day, the Prime Minister said in effect that there are many things the federal government can do on its own on the question of employment this winter. He did not say that is what it is going to do, I appreciate that. He did not say the program it was discussing was going to be exclusively one that should be implemented by the federal government alone in every respect. However, he did say-which is sometimes his wont-what I said which did not answer the question at all. Since then, I have tried to think and understand what the federal government could do to create jobs this winter without the participation of municipal and provincial governments of Canada.
One of the things the federal government could do, Mr. Speaker, is to introduce some meaningful and sizeable tax cuts immediately, affecting the low and low middle income groups in this country. It could do that without consultation with the provinces and the municipalities. I say to the Minister of Finance that this should be done and it should be done immediately. If the government were to come forward with a program to seek tax cuts in addition to those proposed on an inequitable basis in the present tax bill, I am sure that all members of the opposition-and I can speak for members of my own party-

would pass such a bill if it had the effect of cutting taxes for the low and middle income groups in Canada with the least possible debate and in a short time. The purchasing power of the people would thereby be increased immediately for the purpose of stimulating the economy in a very short time. Of course, there is always a time lag between the date tax cuts take place and when their effect is felt on the market and on the economy. We, in our party, would be willing to consider that kind of proposal with the least possible debate, unless it were as horrendous in its inequity as some other proposals which have been produced by the Minister of Finance. Obviously, he does not intend to do any more than is suggested in this tax bill. Otherwise, I cannot understand why he would not already have told us that he intends to make the necessary amendments to the necessary clause of the tax bill in order to produce those tax cuts without delay.
The other thing that I suppose the federal government could do on its own would be to spend some money on its own public works programs. It could build some more fancy, federal office buildings-at least that would produce some jobs. Yet I want to argue this afternoon that I am not interested in make-work proposals. There are necessary things that must be done for the welfare of the people of Canada, and any program of winter jobs ought to be directed towards those objectives.
Even the large amounts of money which might be spent by the Department of Public Works or some other departments of government in connection with programs that the government could undertake would obviously not create many jobs in Canada. I therefore assume, and perhaps I am naive in making this assumption, that any programs for jobs this winter announced by the federal government would include, no matter what else it may or may not include, some money which is to be made available to the provinces or municipalities with respect to various works that the provincial and municipal levels of government may carry out this winter and start immediately. I hope that assumption is correct. If it is not, we will not get a program from the government; we will get a shadow. We will merely get useless suggestions from the federal government for work this winter because the provinces and municipalities will not be involved. I say that because the area in which the federal government, by itself, can produce jobs is so narrow that it will not even touch the issue of unemployment this fall and winter.
I must, therefore, assume, and my colleagues may disagree with me for being so generous, that the government is not unintelligent and that it is sufficiently intelligent to know that it must bring the provinces and municipalities into the picture for any valid, useful and large job creating program. If that is the case, Mr. Speaker, I say to the government that its failure to call an earlier conference on the unemployment question, and I do not care whether the conference was to have been between ministers of finance, treasurers or heads of governments across Canada, was unforgivable. The government ought to have called an earlier federal-provincial conference. Its failure to call that conference last month or, indeed, within the next few weeks, for the purposes of working out collectively a program that would create a massive number of
October 12, 1971

jobs this winter, constitutes a betrayal of its duty to the people of Canada in view of the present unemployment situation and the unemployment situation that is to come.
The Prime Minister has tried to blame other first ministers for the fact that an earlier conference is not being held. According to my reading of the situation, and I have seen the correspondence that has been made public, this government has never asked for and never called a conference to deal with the unemployment situation. The discussions were to be on general economic subjects. If the government intends to make a proposal, present a program or offer some finances in order to create jobs this winter which will involve implementation in part or in whole by provincial and municipal governments, then the present delay on the part of the government in announcing its program is reprehensible. I cannot see how provincial and municipal governments can make ready their plans for jobs in November, December, January and February, if they are not told how much money the government of Canada will make available for that purpose. It should make that known before the end of October, and we are now in the middle of October. The delay, in my humble view, is unforgivable. In my submission, it indicates a hesitation on the part of the government in dealing seriously with the unemployment situation that faces us now and will become more serious in the months ahead. This again indicates the government's failure to consider in human terms this problem affecting millions of Canadians, and its failure to deal sensitively with this massive unemployment situation. It has failed to display the sense of urgency and emergency which the situation requires.
There are no magic ways for dealing with the unemployment situation, Mr. Speaker. Nobody can wave a magic wand and settle these problems. As we discuss this tax bill, the changes in the tax structure which are being made and the inequities which still remain. I wish to put forward some suggestions which I believe are important. First, the government must present a program that will guarantee at least an additional one quarter of a million jobs during the four or five months of winter. Any program that provides additional work for fewer than a quarter of a million of our people will not scratch the surface, since in all likelihood our unemployment this winter will reach well over the half million mark, and perhaps come closer to the three quarters of a million mark, both because of the internal economic situation and because of the reactionary, protectionist Nixon policies of the United States. That is the first point I make, Mr. Speaker. At least a quarter of a million additional jobs must be created by any program that the government will propose.
My second point relates even more directly to the tax bill before us. If it becomes necessary in some way for the government to find the funds which will be necessary for carrying out my suggestion, the government has the responsibility of doing so. My studies and inquiries have shown me that this kind of program cannot be accomplished without a massive injection and expenditure of funds. I am talking of amounts between three quarters of a billion dollars and one billion dollars. Any program that is smaller than that will no more than scratch the surface of the unemployment situation, merely raise the expectations of people which will not be realized and again betray

the desirable as well as justifiable hopes of the Canadian people. They hope that something will be done. I submit that much of this money ought to go into an increased housing program. It ought to develop, particularly, low cost housing both for renters and for those who may be able to buy a house if the down payment is reduced sufficiently, if interest rates are reduced sufficiently and if the income to which the house purchase is related is made more reasonable and practical, in the light of the present situation. I am sure everyone here will agree with me that nothing can create jobs more quickly, and even here there will be quite a time lag, than a massive housing program.
I am aware, and I want to say it before anyone else does-although perhaps nobody else will bother to say this-that housing starts this year have been running at an annual rate of around 220,000, 230,000 or 240,000 units.

Mr. Speaker, the legislation now being discussed has undergone a very long period of gestation. Indeed, in the normal course of things, natural gestation lasts approximately nine months, but that of this pretty legislation, which has a rather impressive thickness, is the fruit of some ten years of labour. And I am convinced that this House does not expect-especially not this government-that it may be passed within a few hours.
I should like, during the few minutes put at my disposal, to review the aspect of this bill which concerns particularly credit unions and co-operatives. That is a most interesting field for us and one that we must consider seriously so as to analyze the legislation now being considered and, if it is passed by this House, to determine its consequences and advantages, if required, so as to make the best possible use of it.
Obviously, the movers of this very complicated legislation should give much more explanations about it so that the interested parties may know its true implications. First there is the whole population, if we think of the important changes brought to the personal income tax act. Then there are the corporations, companies, industrialists, business firms and especially co-operatives and credit unions whose taxation system is running the risk of being radically changed. It is important to look particularly into the amendments suggested for these institutions in this piece of legislation as well as into their demands regarding the system contemplated by the government.
Let us deal first with the co-operatives. We see that the government has introduced two new essential elements in the present taxation system, namely: the principle of capi-
October 12, 1971

tal employed, and new limits on the payment of dividends or refunds.
In practice, for the calculation of the taxable income, the profit, after deduction of dividends or refunds to members, shall not be below 5 per cent of capital employed (i.e. 5 per cent of assets less liabilities), this 5 per cent limit to be reduced only by the inclusion of the amount of interests paid to members. Let us point out that the 3-year exemption period allowed to new co-operatives is completely eliminated.
Under the present system, the limit is not 5 per cent, but 3 per cent, and it allows co-operatives to pay their members, as dividends, a greater part of their profits. Moreover, it is possible to deduct from the 3 per cent, in addition to the interests paid to members, all kinds of interests except those paid to banks and credit unions.
If the legislation is passed as drafted, a greater part of the profits of the co-operative itself will be taxable at the same rate that applies to ordinary corporations, that is 50 per cent, except, of course, for profits under $50,000 that are taxable at 25 per cent, as previously provided.
Therefore, for the same amount of profits reported by co-operatives throughout the country, the government will be able to get significantly higher revenues, while showing no concern about penalizing this way, first, the co-operatives as institutions by depriving them of an important part of the resources they urgently need to expand and, secondly, the hundreds of thousands of members whose individual and collective effort would have been rewarded by these new restrictions in respect of the distribution of benefits or dividends.
To get a clearer view of the probable effects of the government's proposed amendments, let us consider the example of a co-operative whose total capital is $800,000 distributed in round figures as follows: shareholders assets, $500,000; long term debts, carrying interest at 6 per cent, $300,000.
Under the present tax system, this co-operative pays income tax only on profits which, after deduction of dividends, may not be lower than 3 per cent of the total capital, the amount from which it can deduct the interest paid on its long term debt, which breaks down as follows: capital stock, $800,000; shareholders, $500,000; long term debts, $300,000.
Tax is therefore calculated as follows: 3 per cent on $800,000, $24,000; 6 per cent interest on debt of $300,000, $18,000.
After subtracting the taxable profit of $6,000 according to the present table, tax payable would be $1,500.
The situation might change considerably as a result of the propositions contained in Bill C-259. The rate is no longer 3 per cent but 5 per cent and it no longer applies to the total co-operative capital but only to the portion corresponding to the shareholders capital. On the other hand, because of the concept of utilized capital as a basis for calculation of taxable income, the co-operative can no longer deduct from that amount the amount annually allocated to service of the long term debt, and consequently the figures would be the following:
Total capital: $800,000; long-term indebtedness: $300,000, computation of tax: at 5 per cent of $500,000, $25,000; tax payable: 25 per cent of $25,000, $6,250.
Income Tax Act
The taxable amount is therefore increased by $19,000 and the tax payable increases from $1,500 to $6,500, which is over 400 per cent in the case I have just outlined. If, for purposes of normal development, a co-operative decided to provide a mid term, that is a policy for the distribution of patronage dividends, this could lead to an unfortunate situation where a variable part of the co-operative's profits would be taxable at the same time as the dividends legitimately received by its members. Obvioulsy, at the moment the possibility exists, at least in theory, of double taxation. Furthermore, a large part of the dividends are usually re-invested and thus re-integrated into the cooperative's capital and the co-operative can use those funds to buy back the shares of those members who during the year decide to withdraw.
Thus to compel co-operatives to reduce unduly the amount of such dividends could have the following direct consequence: on the one hand, some co-operatives would find it impossible to reimburse their members, and financial and administrative problems would follow, and, on the other hand, to prevent any significant development of a given co-operative which could only rely on its usual income which is absolutely necessary for normal expansion.
That example must be considered as a typical case around which can exist all kinds of intermediate conditions, according to the situation of each co-operative, its importance, its previous commitments, the size of its debt, if necessary, etc.
However, the legislators should be thoroughly convinced that the tax reform proposals of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) are liable to change greatly not only the overall condition of the Canadian co-operative movement, but that of hundreds of co-operatives which have not yet reached the development level enabling them to sustain the heavy blows striken by the new taxing system, unless some of its more controversial aspects are altered.
The authorities and representatives of the various cooperative movements throughout the country have widely taken part in discussions intended to lead to a global tax reform, the principle of which is greater tax equity, so that each category or stratum of society might contribute to the activities of the state according to its respective real possibilities. Needless to say, everyone recognizes that principle and doubtless the leaders and members of the Canadian co-operative movement share it.
Still, that principle, although fundamentally sound and reasonable, must not be laid down as some kind of absolute; it would only lead to rigid positions on the part of the government, and many frustrations for a large sector of the population.
The co-operative movement, if one is to judge by the countless protests against the provisions of clause 135 and the principle of capital employed seems to be one of the main victims of this wish for unconditional tax equality. Co-operative members singled out, in particular, the following points in the bill: the notion of capital employed threatens to reduce considerably the amount of patronage dividends to be paid the members in connection with transactions amongst themselves, and therefore threatens directly the ability for a large number of co-operatives to

reimburse the social capital their members request, and indirectly their ability to expand and develop.
Any further increase in the co-operative's reserves leading to an increase in what has been called the employed capital would mean, rather oddly for that matter, that in a given fiscal year, a co-operative would find itself in the obligation of paying more in income tax although during the same year its real profits had remained static or had decreased. Now that is a wonderful system for the Canadian treasury to collect taxes even when production decreases during the year.
Instead of being forced to adopt the methods of ordinary corporations and to deduct from their taxable income the interest paid on the capital supplied by their members, the co-operatives would like to see their own operating rules respected and to be allowed to keep on distributing their annual operating surplus in the form of patronage dividends.
It must not be forgotten that co-operatives are based on principles and concepts fairly different from what is found in ordinary commercial or industrial corporations. In the first place, a co-operative is an association of men instead of being a simple converging point for capital. The factor "work" and the "collective effort" concept prevail over the notion we consider erroneous of capital for the sake of capital. Men associate to do business, to gain advantages and not first and foremost to make profits. And if the associated individual draws benefits, he must automatically and necessarily take them into account when filing his income tax return and, through the personal income tax return, the government levies the share it wishes each individual to contribute to the financing of the affairs of the state.
The co-operative system can make a large contribution to the improvement or, at least, the humanization of our present capitalist system which is so much criticized in some areas, especially by the youth which will have to accept or reject what they will have been left with by the preceding generation.
If this principle of fiscal equality, which is generally recognized and which is not endangered by any serious threat because it is accepted by everybody, is furthered too blindly and perhaps too rapidly, it would be rather surprizing to see the government commit by the same occasion serious inequities by not amending the discriminatory measures toward the co-operative movement that it is about to have passed by this House. These measures do not take into account either the characteristics or the methods particular to the co-operative associations. The new taxation pattern does not seem to correspond with their specific nature and will force them to relinquish their distinct characteristics or simply disappear as co-operative associations as such. A fiscal mechanism would be introduced in the relationship between the co-operative and its members by modifying the redistribution pattern of surpluses which is peculiar to co-operatives. Because of this mechanism, they would be forced to contravene the laws by which they are regulated.
There is here, at the very least, an obvious contradiction, all the more as the House, through the Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs Standing Committee had
[Mr. Lambert (Bellechasse).j
expressed the wish, when considering the white paper on tax reform, that while no tax concession should be granted to organizations such as co-operatives, in the future, their activities should not be hindered nor should they be heavily taxed.
It is therefore a question of vested interests, and it would be prejudicial, to say the least, that in wanting to be too fair on one particular point, we were grossly unfair on other aspects of the same problem. We therefore suggest that the government, while not overlooking the basic purpose of tax reform, introduce the new taxation system of corporations gradually and selectively, unless it is willing to reconsider on the whole the first clauses of Bill C-259.
The step that the co-operatives are asked to take appears definitely too big, and many of them, not so well organized or more recent, may simply disappear, and this would kill the co-operative movement, which would not be questioned. Special consideration should be given to consumer co-operatives with rather small assets and that are non profit-making.
In addition to this progressive concept, it would also be logical to establish some selective feature, so that all cooperatives would not be on an equal footing and some effort would be made to take into account, among other things, the development level of each one, and that in this way some consideration would be given according to fair and realistic criteria, to the tendency of each to compete with corporations or ordinary commercial and industrial firms, since that is the fundamental argument brought forward by the latter.
It may be correct to state that some co-operatives, super co-ops, realize some very substantial profits on which they should be taxed accordingly, especially where they are competing with ordinary companies which do not enjoy the same tax privileges. This situation should obviously be straightened out, which is perfectly in line with the guiding principles of any tax reform which is to be equitable. But there is a risk of losing sight of this principle of equity, if the same provisions should apply fully to several hundreds of co-operatives which have not yet reached a degree of development allowing them to bear the burden of these new tax measures. In those cases we would run the risk of destroying the very spirit of the co-operative movement which it was so difficult for us to inculcate upon the people. Therefore we should not chance freezing or paralysing a basically sound and human sector of our economy by being adamant on a principle concerning tax reform.
Not only co-operatives are endangered by the measures proposed by the Minister of Finance. Caisses populaires and credit unions are running the risk of being squeezed out before long because the bill remains very uncertain about the tax system that will be applied to them. Those institutions themselves have recognized that they should, from now on, be taxed according to their profits. Anyway, they will be taxed on the same basis as corporations, which is, at a rate of 25 per cent on profits up to $50,000, and of 50 per cent on those in excess of this figure-which will be a substantial change from the non-taxation position in which they have been to this day.
However, those organizations are asking for the establishment of a basically fair taxation system-a system
October 12, 1971

Income Tax Act
which would not open the way to situations of double taxation. In this connection, it is recommended that interest paid to members, as well as the amount of compulsory reserves accumulated under provincial laws, be deductible from the income of caisses populaires. By only allowing deduction of so-called normal reserves, the amount of which they would set in arbitrary fashion, the federal government might run counter to well established provincial laws which set the amount of such reserves at a higher level. In my opinion, we must avoid creating such
distortions in the various measures that rule the activities of Canadians, whether it concerns co-operatives or credit unions. Reducing the amount of tax deductible reserves will unfortunately oblige those institutions to pay smaller dividends to their members. Another consequence of the proposed legislation will be to force former members of credit unions to get credit elsewhere at considerably higher rates.
On the one hand, we therefore risk further choking the small wage earner who greatly benefits from the healthy operation of the credit institution to which he belongs and, on the other hand, as is the case for co-operatives, we seem to forget the judicial nature of credit unions and caisses populaires. We would thus tend to deprive them of their co-operative status to consider them as banks or finance companies. As a matter of fact, if caisses populaires enjoyed the same privileges as chartered banks, as far as creating money is concerned, I might then think they could pay income tax as banks do, but that is not the case. A caisse populaire does not have the power to create money, therefore it cannot make any profit on the creation of credit or exploit it. It can only lend its members' money. I want to point out that the shares of the members of such institutions should not be considered as the equivalent of shares in a company since they are, in principle, redeemable any time and constitute, for all practical purposes, a saving which clause 137 of omnibus Bill C-259 does not seem to recognize.
We suggest that the government specify as quickly as possible in a clearer language the points that are still obscure in some clauses with regard to the taxation system applied to caisses populaires and credit unions in order that these institutions may know exactly what they can expect from the federal tax system, even if only to help them better plan their activities on short, middle and long terms. Among the points which require clarification there are the deduction of dividends on the authorized capital before computation of the taxable income and the status of investments made by credit unions. We will have to revise as in the case of co-operatives, the concept of used capital and to remove for credit unions the obligation of doing business in a single province, as is presently the case, since from now on they will be taxed on the same basis as any other corporation. Finally, the credit unions should be authorized to invest in municipal, school board and Crown corporation bonds.
Many credit unions, Mr. Speaker, have been established at the cost of a great many scarifices on the part of initiators, because they had to cope with many difficulties, namely poverty in the parochial environment, where promoters wanted to establish a caisse populaire to serve the local population.
I can well remember the establishment of a Caisse in a new settlement even though headquarters which were authorized to decide whether a caisse could be established in such or such a parish, had dimissed the idea on account of the poverty of the people. So the promoters organized a party to raise the funds required by headquarters, to pay the expenses of an agent and enable him to proceed to the establishment of the caisse in that parish.
That, Mr. Speaker, is a proof of the confidence bestowed upon the Caisses populaires and the proof of great dedication, showing the earnestness with which people may want a credit union in their area. The travelling expenses of a responsible person, authorized to open such a caisse, are defrayed.
And that is what actually happened. That man went to the parish and the Caisse was established. For 30 years now it has rendered innumerable services to the community there and still serves it.
That goes to show that Caisses populaires are most of the time the outcome of dedication and sacrifice. That is why I deem unfortunate that this government, who have a pressing need for money, due to the wasting in many cases of public funds, should be obliged to bring forward a tax reform under which the co-operative movement, caisses populaires and credit unions are equally taxed.
As regards most of the Caisses, managers worked voluntarily at the outset of operations. More than once, I have seen a manager working full time as a voluntary worker, for a 12, 24 or 36-month period, in order that the caisse may survive and provide the services that people were expecting.
The administrators, the counsellors, the credit officials have been working and are still working without pay. Dedication alone made a success of the Mouvement Cooperatif Desjardins as well as of other co-operative movements which have benefited from many people's dedication, whether they be professionals, businessmen, workers, or farmers and all of them have given their time to run those co-operatives which have rendered many services to our citizens.
I say it is absolutely necessary to take into account the social role played by co-operatives and caisses populaires instead of considering only the material aspect of the situation and therefore considering them as corporations and applying an unconditional tax levelling which would not be necessarily beneficial to the community. These organizations where a great deal of free dedication is prevailing, are moreover a guaranty of stability against the ever-increasing control of our economy by foreign big business and this is why we should not hinder them unduly. Recently, we again witnessed the dedication and enterprise of co-operatism.
Part of the Gaspe population is facing a difficult situation. Thanks to organizations like the Catholic Farmers' Union and other co-operative organizations, they want to set up a cardboard factory at Cabano to make use of the environmental natural resources, that is the broad-leaved trees, to produce cardboard since they are assured of being able to sell that production in certain European countries. This firm is presently facing a situation so difficult that the issue was raised in an article published

by the newspaper Le Soleil of Wednesday, October 6, 1971, and I quote:
Without the help of the government, the Cabano cardboard factory will be taken over by foreign interests.
Mr, Speaker, the factory has not been established yet and one can already foresee foreign interests taking over its operations and profits.
This is why, as I say, we must be careful before passing this bill so we do not nip in the bud those projects resulting from the initiative of people anxious to render great services to the province and the country. We must rather allow this project to become reality and make sure that those people get the services that they have a right to expect.
I hope, Mr. Spaker, that the minister will be prepared to give those thoughts due consideration and propose himself the necessary amendments. I also wish to point out to the government that it is not good for the Canadian economy to tax too heavily private enterprise for it will only discourage those who have initiative and talent for business. Unfortunately, we hear too often businessmen say, why strive to develop a business or an industry because the government takes away through taxation too large a share of those profits we have worked so hard for.
Recently the Canadian Chamber of Commerce held a congress during which its president stated the following:
The business heads must act more vigorously to avoid new legislation putting an end to their operations.
Never in the course of our history have the skills of Canadian businessmen enabling them to efficiently manage their enterprises, provide for expansion, make a reasonable profit and sustain competition been so severely put to test by legislation.
If the excessive burden and the interference of governments are not alleviated, our businessmen will no longer be in a position to exercise their main functions, that is to promote business and ensure economic development.
Mr. Speaker, here we have the president of a Canadian organization who, in very clear terms, sounds the alarm to warn all Canadian businessmen that the situation is dangerous and tell the government that it is taking the wrong direction and risks, through its legislation, discouraging, as I said a while ago, all those talented men of goodwill who really want to make their contribution to Canada's economic development. That is a warning, I might say, that should be heeded by the government.
The important question is the following: Then, how can the country's expenses be financed if co-operatives, caisses populaires and private enterprise are already fully taxed? The government needs money. Where will it get it? Here is a very wise solution, a solution that ought to be applied one of these days, and the sooner the better.
Here it is: a tax reform is more pressing than ever, but we should first have a monetary reform to modify the method of financing the public sector. Greater use of the Bank of Canada is imperative for the creation of new credits entailing administration charges only as interest, which would greatly lower government expenditures.
This afternoon, in answer to the question of my colleague, the member for Compton (Mr. Latulippe), who asked him whether he felt that the Bank of Canada should reduce its interest rates that chartered banks might lower theirs in order to give our economic activities a new impulse and reduce inflation, the Prime Minister
(Mr. Lambert (Bellechasse).j
(Mr. Trudeau) replied very candidly that the rates of interest are set by the Bank of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, is the Bank of Canada an institution of Parlement? Should it not submit itself to the instructions of the government? One may also ask whether it is subject to the whims of chartered banks. If that is the case, then neither the government nor the bank can decide, but rather chartered banks which have the privilege of controlling credit in the country and making the most of it to their advantage while penalizing everybody else.
It is against this state of affairs that we protest; as long as it lasts, it will be our duty to warn the government that they are not entirely in the right direction and if they are able then to take steps to reform or change the present institutions, we will be here to approve them.
I was listening in this very House, a few days ago, to the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) speaking about an international monetary reform. I support him, but if we proceeded first with a domestic monetary reform, this would contribute to the solution of international problems.
Mr. Speaker, I would have much more to say. I could speak about taxes affecting individuals and families as such. I have no time to analyse today this aspect of the bill, but I shall come back to it at the report stage to lay down the rights of individuals and families and show once more that these categories of people are overburdened with taxes and cannot enjoy a secure and free normal life.
