subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate on this tax bill is almost an anti-climax. What seemed so important this past few years, the long awaited revision of our tax structure, has been dwarfed by a single national issue, the future of Canadian-American relations. The average Canadian may not know a great deal about the complexities of international fiscal affairs, but there is no doubt that there is a feeling in the land that the Ottawa experts, politicians and mandarins alike, have critically miscalculated the United States reaction to its own problems. There has been the government's failure to solve inflation, plus the employment crisis. There has been an obvious lack of effective communication between Ottawa and Washington. This has not been helped in any way by the Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau) obvious hostility toward the Americans. There is substantial evidence, and it is feared by all, that we may well be led into another great depression.
The problem with this tax bill is that it is tailored to a decade that has passed. It is perhaps perverse misfortune that the tax review and tax changes have come at the beginning of the decade of the seventies. Ever since 1968 there has been slow, vague, but unmistakable evidence that equity was not the only prerequisite for tax changes. The mere scrapping of much of the white paper on taxation indicates that the government, I believe much against its will, has given some recognition to the necessity of economic growth.
What are the two most important things that have to be considered in relating the tax bill to our economic needs? The crux for Canada falls into two main problems at the internal level. The first is that Canada has the fastest growing labour force relative to population in the western world, but the cost of creating jobs for those entering the labour force is on the rise. The investment required to create a new job in conventional manufacturing is around $25,000, and in advanced, technological manufacturing around $75,000. Technological advance accelerates the investment required to create jobs with each passing day.
Much of our trouble is a consequence of a sharp rise in the birth rate a generation ago, something for which even the politicians cannot be blamed. A decade from now policies and social attitudes will need to be altered to take account of an opposite situation, a slowing of the labour force growth resulting from a steep fall in the birth rate since the early 1960's. Indeed the present taxation proposals might well be more applicable ten years from now than they are in the decade of the seventies. A perusal of birth rates indicates an increase from 1956, when there were 461,000 births, to a figure of 479,000 births in 1960, followed by a steady drop to 362,000 in 1968. So, it can be seen that there will be a large number of young people entering the labour force during the seventies, estimated by some people as between 21 million and 3 million. Whether or not jobs will be created for them will depend on our economic system, on the stimulus that business, both private and government, can generate to create new jobs. In my opinion, the effect of this tax bill will not be nearly sufficient to have this result.
Income Tax Act
There are other interesting developments in our society that may have an influence on this group now coming into the labour market. The finding of jobs for this group will be difficult. Many may remain unemployed, or at least under-employed, for a great part of their lives. The trend towards education may turn some of these people into so-called perennial students, at least until they are in their thirties or even forties. The rise of the drug culture, and an increase in the so-called hippies or drop-outs, may be larger than usual. Indeed, it may well be that many of the people who were born in the 1950's and 1960's will never really be gainfully employed, at least in the context experience by those born prior to that time.
There is little we can do about the numbers entering the work force, unless by some control on immigration, but there is something that we could do through this bill about the second most important feature of our economy in the seventies. I refer to the enormous welfare costs that we have experienced, that we are going to experience, and that will expand even further. I think it is important to give careful thought to the proposed tax changes because it is fairly obvious that the new tax structure will have to generate the revenues to carry the welfare system. Successive federal governments have laid the foundation for and erected most of the structure of the most comprehensive and generous welfare scheme in existence. Generating the income to finance it is already straining our resources. Perhaps the awareness of this fact had something to do with the crunch issue in tax reform-economic growth versus social equity. I believe that the recognition of these two main facets of our Canadian life in the seventies has to be considered when we discuss changes in the taxation system.
The high costs of government are nowhere more apparent than in the latest official projection of Statistics Canada. This year governments collectively will claim revenues amounting to about 46 per cent of the nation's total production of goods and services, or 42 per cent if pensions and hospital premiums are excluded from the accounts. It seems that when new government departments are established, or old ones upgraded, they must produce programs costing many millions of dollars if they are to be taken seriously. Sometimes one program is put forward as a substitute for another. For example, family allowances were notably wasteful. Much of the money went to people who did not need it. Under the revision undertaken by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) they will certainly be more purposeful, and this will cost the taxpayers $150 million more the first year. Again, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) has taken some of the insurance out of unemployment insurance. The creation of jobs and the control of government spending will be most important in the decade of the seventies. This tax bill does not in any way recognize the needs of the decade. Even if the bill deviates from the white paper, it would appear to be far too equity orientated and not growth orientated.
There are numerous ways in which this tax bill could be upgraded into a more useful document. I would like to enumerate a few of the areas in which this legislation is deficient. The first obvious area is that of unincorporated

October 12, 1971
Income Tax Act
business. This comprises somewhere in the neighbourhood of a million to two million Canadians, and includes the many small storekeepers, the small entrepreneurs, tradesmen and farmers. The new income tax legislation absolutely ignores them because the income tax group in which most of these people would fall will be more heavily taxed than previously.
The progressive income tax is orientated to those who are consumers alone and not to those who must, after their income tax is paid, provide the capital necessary to carry on their small farm, their business or their enterprise. We have heard much about the movement of people in Canada from rural to urban areas. Because this individual, unincorporated entrepreneur is so important to rural investment in Canada, because we are a nation with a sparse population scattered over many hundreds of square miles, we must pay, economically and socially, more attention to this group. The present tax bill will do nothing for these individual businessmen and farmers, and I believe that this is a pity.
Recognition is given to some extent to people who invest in large companies by means of dividend tax credits, but nothing is changed or improved for the group of people who are the unincorporated businessmen. This is a pity because even the most rabid believer in government does not see the small, unincorporated business person or farmer as a cartel or a threat to the economic well-being of Canada.
I would point out that those people who are on salary or wages are in positions where the capital which is provided is sustained by other means than their own, and are in a preferred position as opposed to the unincorporated businessman so far as capital is concerned. These salary or wage people have the option of saving or not saving after their income tax is paid, but this is not so for the unincorporated businessman who must, out of his income after his income tax is paid, provide the capital necessary for the expansion and sustenance of his small enterprise.
This is an area in which the tax bill does nothing, and indeed with the increased tax that most people in this $5,000 to $20,000 bracket will pay as a result of the inauguration of the capital gains tax, they will be worse off than they were previously. As the capital investment needed to provide income increases, the proposed tax structure, so far as these people are concerned, is a retrogressive step. Mr. Speaker, these people should receive more attention from the country to weather the international situation which we are facing and provide a reasonable standard of living without absolute reliance on international trade and finance.
I would next turn, Mr. Speaker, to what I feel is a serious defect in the tax bill and that is the treatment of the small, incorporated business. In my opinion, the treatment accorded the small incorporated business is really no treatment at all from a tax point of view. This is understandable considering that the revenue department expected that the great bulk of the increase in revenue needed to make up for the reduction in the personal income tax would come as a result of the changes in the tax structure relating to small incorporated business. This perhaps explains why the tax department has virtually made a mockery out of the suggestions from the Parliamentary Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic
(Mr. Ritchie.J
Affairs which, having heard a great number of representations, suggested that the reduced rate of income tax on the first $35,000 of the profits of an incorporated business was valuable in our economy. Mr. Speaker, the new tax changes would indicate that while the government is paying lip service to an accumulation of capital by the small incorporated business it in effect is effectively preventing the function of this most important facet.
From personal experience, I know that many small incorporated businesses are incorporated solely because of the limited liability feature in the event of bankruptcy. Having studied, in a personal way, the tax structure of small incorporated businesses, I can see very little advantage in the long run, so far as taxation is concerned, in having the business incorporated if the company does not expand. It was useful for a company that was expanding rapidly and needed a fair amount of capital generation. What is wrong with the present proposals? Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that they are too complex and too vague to be of much value. If a company had a good growth pattern, and this I believe is what is needed in our economy, the owner would be discouraged from taking advantage of the reduced taxation on the first $50,000 because it would severely limit his ability to manoeuvre in the future.
I would regard this portion of the tax reform measure as being extremely retrogressive, and if the government feels that the reduced taxation of the first $50,000 of income is good for the economy on the one hand, then it has largely reversed itself by hedging this feature with so many restrictions that it will lose much of its value. If the government intends to restrict the sale of Canadian companies to foreign countries, which is synonymous with America, they are going about it in a heavy-handed way. Whatever we may decide about American capital in Canada, this particular device of preventing the sale of Canadian industry does not seem valuable. Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that the various restrictions on tax relief for small businesses are so confining that they defeat the purpose of furthering business incentive in a substantial way.
Turning now to the effect of the tax bill on Canada's extractive industries, I would like to say a few words on this subject, Mr. Speaker. Much has been said by the economic nationalists to the effect that every bit of ore mined in Canada should be fully manufactured into consumer goods before being exported. Indeed, it would seem that the economic nationalists believe that we are able to do this. They say that the great employment opportunities are in manufacturing but, Mr. Speaker, Canadian manufacturing, no matter how you look at it, is, on balance, a high cost industry. The extractive industries, the pulp and paper industry and the agriculture industry, have allowed the people of Canada to accumulate the wealth to consume the products that our high priced manufacturing industry produces. Without the exports from the resource industries, there would be a much smaller manufacturing industry in Canada than now exists.
From my observations of the mining industry and the oil and gas industry while on the parliamentary Finance Committee, I would assert that taxation is a cost of doing business. If we increase the taxes, the mining industry will contract; if we decrease the taxes, the mining industry will expand. Assuming that there is a market for the
October 12, 1971

products mined, it seems obvious that increased taxes can only be borne when the price of the mineral rises on the domestic or international market or that more lucrative grades of ore only will be mined. If the tax on the resource industries is substantially increased and there is not a corresponding increase in the price on the international market of that product, then mining will decline. There may be some argument for the contraction of mining as a conservation measure but I think it should be achieved apart from the taxation structure.	*
Perhaps what makes the debate on resource taxation so obscure is that the areas dependant on the resource industries are so far removed from the high population centres of Montreal and Toronto. Mining towns in my province of Manitoba, like Lynn Lake, Flin Flon and Thompson, would not exist without ore to be mined and a market found for it. On September 21, the Globe and Mail, reported Mr Goodeve, Treasurer of McIntyre Porcupine Mines Limited as having said:
The tax reform package will make the development of new mines less attractive by lowering the return on mining investment. Certain marginal mines, which would be economic under present conditions, will no longer be viable under the new tax regime.
But these effects probably will not be felt immediately because the new system is to be phased in gradually. 'The most basic uncertainty regarding the new provisions relates to exploration, yet its impact will be more immediate because the investment decisions which must be made now are concerned not with the short-term but with the eventual rates of return from discoveries not yet made, which must compare favourably with investment opportunities elsewhere.'
I think that Mr. Goodeve has made a signification charge against the taxation bill and it is up to the government to prove that his statements are wrong. Similarly, in oil and gas, the proposed taxation changes have been accepted only to the extent that they are much less punitive than the original white paper.
It has been estimated that the oil and gas industry of western Canada has provided for a million more people on the Prairies than we would presently have. When it is remembered that that industry was almost completely developed with American and western Canadian capital, and that the eastern financial groups showed no interest in western oil for many years, I think we have to look carefully at the effect of increasing the flow of taxes to Ottawa and correspondingly decreasing those to the provinces. Last year the estimated reserves of oil, excluding the tar sands, in Alberta, the main oil producing province, declined. This decrease it is suggested came about largely because the White Paper on Taxation caused cessation of drilling and exploration. Mr. Speaker, we hear much of Canadians being hewers of wood and drawers of water for the Americans. By this tax bill the government has indicated that it wants western Canadians especially to be hewers of wood and drawers of water for central Canada. Although we may have our problems with the Americans, at least we can control them politically in western Canada. The same cannot be said for the Ottawa, Montreal, Toronto axis.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in its statement on co-operatives, the government has adopted a very severe attitude. It is particularly damaging to the prairie regions because of the
Income Tax Act
great importance of producers' co-operatives in that area. The government's proposal will be damaging for all regions. I wish to speak mainly about producer co-operatives and about wheat pools, which are co-operatives. In order to raise the taxes that will be imposed on the wheat pools of the three prairie provinces, which are involved in grain handling there will have to be a substantial increase in the handling charges on grain. This will come at a time of particularly severe crisis in the western economy.
There are great discussions about the need for modernization of the western grain handling industry and massive expenditures would seem to be necessary for this. This particular taxation change, in so far as it effects the wheat pools, means that if the western grain industry is to be modernized, there will have to be a drastic increase in the handling charges for grain. Mr. Speaker, in effect the farmers are going to be hit by a double blow. As it is, the Wheat Pools are responsible for about 50 per cent of the grain handling volume in western Canada. In any case, the farmers will have to pay for modernization of the grain handling system by increased tariffs on grain and, as well, provide massive increases of money for the cooperatives to meet the new tax levies. As well, other producer co-operatives that provide a service to the western farm industry are similarly concerned.
The co-operatives and credit unions, Mr. Speaker, have stated their case most forcibly to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), and I would hope that some reason will prevail. There are substantial ways and means by which the taxation of co-operatives could be changed. I would hope that there will be a full discussion of these clauses at the proper time, that the government will introduce appropriate amendments and at least be more reasonable with regard to its tax on co-operatives and credit unions.
There are a good many areas in the bill which, in a minor way, could be attacked. Those areas are severely restrictive of growth. I refer to areas such as depreciation allowances for buildings, which I feel are too severe, although I admit certain changes ought to have been made. These should be depreciation allowances for buildings different from those brought forward. There needed to be changes in that high income individuals have been able to buy, say, apartment blocks without any fear of having to pay tax. Yet I submit that the clause dealing with this is far too severe. The government seems to have brought forward a cannon, whereas a peashooter would have been much better in this situation. I think, as time goes on, it will be shown that clauses such as this are very restrictive and will impede the growth of small businesses, particularly in the smaller communities.
There is, however, a final and important area that I should like to talk about, namely, the proposal for the taxing of our international accounts. It would appear that the government wishes to renegotiate the tax treaties so that it can levy a tax on capital gains on defined Canadian property and offer to restrict Canada's withholding tax on investment and passive income to 15 per cent, in place of the 25 per cent provided for in the new tax legislation, in the years after 1975. The proposed new legislation significantly changes the treatment of investments by Canadian taxpayers in the shares of non-resident corporations that could be described as foreign affiliates. The present provisos regarding dividends which are deductible in comput-

Income Tax Act
ing taxable incomes received by Canadian corporations from a non-resident corporation in which the Canadian corporation holds more than 25 per cent of the voting shares would be narrowed considerably after 1975. The proposed new law provides that after 1975 only dividends from foreign affiliates in countries with which Canada has a new tax treaty will be deductible in computing taxable income. The proposed new law also includes in a Canadian taxpayer's income an arbitrary amount of "property income" with respect to each of the taxpayer's foreign affiliates. The rules are painted with a broad brush but appear quite arbitrary. The new provisions treat the "passive income" derived from foreign investments more harshly and, in effect, penalize non-operating business incomes.
The proposed law also provides that the capital gains of a non-resident will be taxable. Finally, after 1975, foreign tax credit on the investment income of individuals will be limited to 15 per cent, with the excess being treated only as a deductible expense. In view of the various moves by the United States which will encourage production and investment at home, Bill C-259 is totally inappropriate. Canada is threatening to increase the rate of withholding tax on investment and passive income to non-residents to 25 per cent, just when we need more savings and investment to replace the gap that will be left by the United States programs. Further, the proposed capital gains tax on foreign investments would be more onerous than that imposed by the United States.
Why should foreigners invest in Canada when better tax treatment is available? Canada is hoping to pressure other countries into re-negotiating tax treaties when these other countries are beset by serious global monetary problems. At this time, when it is important for Canada to establish new opportunities to make up for less investments from the U.S., we are going out of our way to antagonize alternative markets and sources of capital. We are penalizing, too, foreign affiliates of Canadian companies, so that retaliation will ensue.
Under the tax bill, foreign affiliates of a Canadian company would have their profits taxed in Canada at the same rate as if the manufacturing were carried on in Canada. This could put such corporations at a disadvantage, compared to other companies located outside Canada. If the foreign affiliate were located in country X with a 20 per cent corporate tax rate, other companies located in country X would be paying taxes at the 20 per cent rate, but not Canadian companies. At a time when virtually everyone agrees that Canada can get the required scale and specialization to compete internationally only through the development of its own multi-national corporations, the tax bill offers nothing. In fact, as mentioned previously, there are positive handicaps offered to such companies which would be severe roadblocks.
I should like to quote from John Meyer's column in the Montreal Gazette of October 12, 1971. He said this about the American surcharge:
On the other hand, some of the conditions-at least two of them-would be very much to Canada's advantage to acknowledge. The first of these is an end to the discrimination against
foreign investors, and Canadians investing abroad, which is written into the tax reform legislation.
There never should have been that discrimination in the first place. We'd be wise to get rid of it.
He goes on with other points. This tax bill will not, in my opinion, provide adequate stimulus for jobs in Canada in this decade. It tends to favour the manufacturing industries of central Canada at the expense of the periphery of the country. It assumes that manufacturing is better than resource development per se. At a time when the countries of the world are becoming more interdependent on one another, it assumes that Canadians should look inward. Since the present federal government has its head in Montreal, perhaps it is only natural that it is carrying on a 200-year exploitation as in the days of the Northwest Trading Company, whose line extended out of Montreal through the Ottawa valley and on through Winnipeg, the Prairies and the mountains to the Pacific ocean.
This tax bill will only increase the tendency to fragmentize our country. To western Canadians, the pull of the continent is north and south. The tax bill does not recognize this in any way. Indeed, how could it, considering the authors? it is an inward looking document and will not greatly enhance the goal of a strong independent Canada.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext:
In taking part in the debate this afternoon on Bill C-259, Mr. Speaker, it seems that one of the major issues and difficulties facing the House at this time is the unintelligibility of this bill. There are many people in this country who do not completely understand what this bill means. I am one of those who do not completely understand all the implications of it.
As we proceed, many members will be forced to vote on provisions of a bill that is very difficult to understand. One tax consultant, Mr. Ferguson, conceded in the August issue of Canadian Business:
Most people in the business world think this law is a great improvement over the White Paper. Whether we are right or not may take years to learn. After all, we are still having appeals about the interpretation of the 1948 law. This new Tax Reform Bill will prove no easier to interpret, and without any question it will be much more difficult for the Department of National Revenue to administer.
More re-writing of the Income Tax Act is not too many years in the future.
Another specialist has summed up this bill with regard to its intelligibility as follows:
Have you been puzzled by the strange silence since Mr. Benson's tax reform Bill was published?
We really have not heard as much about the bill as we did about the white paper.
The reason is that people are waiting for the tax experts to tell them what it means. But after two months of intense study the tax experts are still stupefied with bewilderment.
Well, you may say, so the tax experts are not as clever as they thought. If they have to work a little harder, what's wrong with that? If the tax experts are suffering some temporary agony, they richly deserve it. Besides, they will be more than adequately paid for their trouble.
Unfortunately, things are not this simple. First let me explain that I am not complaining about that kind of tax reforms Mr. Benson wants to give us. I agree with most of those reforms. At least I think I do. The trouble is, I can't tell if the Bill says what Mr. Benson says it does. The Bill is so huge, so complicated, and so badly drafted that it is almost unreadable.
|Mr. Ritchie.]
October 12, 1971

An example of the Bill's tortuous wording is the section describing what a capital gain is. That section, number 39, is about half a page long. As statutes go, that isn't too bad. However, after reading four lines, the reader is directed to turn back to section 3 and read in another page of type. If this were not bad enough, you are told at the same time to read section 3 as though it said the opposite of what it does say.
Rather strange circumstances, Mr. Speaker.
The explanation for this, I think, is that the draftsman, working under great pressure, took what to him was a helpful shortcut. He probably understands what he was saying. But, for several years afterwards, taxpayers, their advisers and judges will have to do these mental gymnastics a thousand times over. Little drafting shortcuts like these are going to cost the country a great deal.
I know that many will say that the tax experts are merely adding hypocrisy to their other sins by complaining. But we are not so selfish and irresponsible as to believe that an economic bonanza for us is necessarily good for the country. None of us want to be the beneficiaries of a law which imposes a higher than necessary compliance cost on the rest of society. As Canadians, we want the laws to be such that most people can understand and comply with them without the constant attendance of a professional adviser.
Everyone knows the amount of money it takes to hire professional help to complete an income tax return.
Few people realize it, but the weakest link in the legislative process is legal drafting. Statute-drafting is the least glamorous and most exacting work a lawyer can have. As a result, practitioners of the art are few, under-valued and grossly over-worked. This, combined with the pressure to get large volumes of legislation through Parliament as quickly as possible, produces many laws which are unclear.
Usually these shortcomings don't matter too much. Most statutes, after all, touch directly only a few people or, if they apply widely, affect one only infrequently. Judges, lawyers and government officials manage to make the laws work reasonably well most of the time. The nuisance and expense occasioned by flaws in a statute are rarely a major problem.
There is a difference between income tax law and criminal law, for instance, Mr. Speaker. It is more necessary that income tax law be easily understood since it affects almost everyone in the country at one time or another. It seems to me that legislation of this sort should be framed with precision and at the same time made as simple as possible. Any cost occasioned businessmen or manufacturers in filling out complicated tax returns will be added to the cost of the products they sell; indeed, there is no other way in which they can reimburse themselves. Thus, any errors or complications in this legislation will cost a great deal of money in the future. The legislation may be a bonanza for our lawyers and accountants but I expect it will cause them a good many headaches too. Many people have contended that this bill should be rewritten. In view of the attitude of the government, I do not think this is likely; the government has already proven it wants the bill passed.
The impetus for this tax legislation came from the Carter commission set up a few years ago by a former government. The commission reported in 1967 and proposed many changes. Then the government published a white paper entitled "Proposals for Tax Reform", I believe in November 1969. I am sure all members are familiar with the response made to that white paper. Thousands of submissions on it were sent to Members of Parliament and to the minister. As I recall, he had to hire staff to help him answer the submissions that were made.
Income Tax Act
The House of Commons Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, and also the Senate Committee on Banking, Trade and Commerce, heard many submissions and held hearings across Canada on the white paper. The findings of these committees were reported back to Parliament and, I think, acknowledged to a certain extent in the legislation now before us. Certainly the minister seems to have listened to some of them. I believe he has also listened to many of the representations of Conservative members on this side of the House. Compared with the proposals in the white paper, the legislation before us is a considerable modification.
Some parts of the legislation particularly concern me and I should like to turn to these now. One concern is how the legislation will affect farmers. I should like to give hon. members a rundown on the hardships farmers will suffer under the legislation. Farmers and fishermen will still be able to compute their income on a cash basis, as they always have. They will still be entitled to use the averaging basis for computing income, which means they can average their income over any five-year period that they may choose.
Under the former law a farmer could classify his cattle as a basic herd. Any gains or losses would be treated as a capital gain or a capital loss and such gains would be exempt from tax. Under the present bill the basic herd and straight line depreciation provisions will be eliminated and livestock farmers will have until December 31 this year to establish their basic herd. Following that, any gain on the basic herd will be tax free but no new additions to the herd will be allowed. In addition, assets acquired after December 31 must be depreciated in accordance with the diminishing balance system. If proceeds from the sale of assets depreciated on a straight line basis exceed their valuation, then the amount of the excess is regarded as a capital gain.
I think this will be the greatest hardship the farming community will suffer under the new legislation. At the present time a farmer can purchase a combine or a tractor, and since it has a motor it is depreciated at the rate of 20 per cent. Therefore, in five years this machinery would have been completely depreciated. At the same time, it would retain some commercial value and could be traded in on a new machine. In turn, this would mean another farmer who could not afford a new machine could buy a used one. This was regarded as a capital gain and the farmer did not have to pay tax on the amount he realized on the machine.
Under the provisions of the new legislation the proceeds of sale will be taxed as a capital gain, and as I understand the situation the farmers will be very reluctant to trade in any machine for a new one if it still has some commercial value. This will mean that the machinery manufacturing companies will lose business and their employees will suffer. In addition, more farmers will look to custom combining instead of purchasing their own machines. I believe this will be one of the major hardships suffered by farmers under the legislation.
Other capital gains will also be subject to tax. Hobby farmers will be able to deduct only $5,000 of any loss incurred. In this regard I wish to raise a grievance with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) or, more particularly, with the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gray).

October 12, 1971
Income Tax Act
Some tax offices want to be assured in black and white that losses claimed by farmers for income tax purposes did occur in anticipation of their making a gain. It is sometimes quite difficult for the farmers to do this and some of the income tax offices, particularly the one in Kitchener, have been very difficult in this regard. Even when reasonable proof has been furnished, the attitude of these offices has caused farmers tremendous hardship. The offices say the tax will be given back when the farmers actually show a profit as anticipated. This represents a considerable hardship for those involved.
In a general way, any advantages to farmers in respect of income tax will be wiped out under this reform, and we all know that the agricultural industry is not tremendously prosperous. It is an industry which under this government, is engaged in providing cheap food for the rest of the country. I do not believe that is a proper activity in which farmers should be engaged. They should be entitled to as much income as people who belong to unions and will not work for less than $5 per hour.
Valuation day will prove to be another difficult time for farmers. I am not sure I can be in favour of a capital gains tax in view of the situation in which we find ourselves in this country. This is a young country which requires growth and risk capital to develop in the manner we would like. Under the capital gains regulations in the bill a farmer will be allowed an amount similar to that allowed a person owning a house in the city, in accordance with the terms of the white paper. Under this silly recommendation in the white paper they were to be allowed $1,000. This simply means that a lot of people would be doing a great deal of bookkeeping for nothing.
Since the white paper and the presentation of this legislation, that condition has been wiped out for home owners. It has been left in respect of the farmer, who can have a gain of $1,000 on his house, a barn and an acre or so of land, free of capital gains tax, but pay capital gains tax on the rest of the farm. A great many farmers have more than one house and a barn, but the legislation states that only the house the farmer lives in, one barn and a few acres may be exempt from capital gains tax. The change I suggest is that all the buildings on the farm, whether they be one or two sets of buildings, four, five or 20 sets of buildings, should be exempt from capital gains tax.
An article in the Globe and Mail of July 1 suggested that a farmer whose children did not want to carry on the family farm would have to sell his assets and pay capital gains tax on $50,000, for example. He might then reinvest his capital in the market, liquidate three or four years later and find that so far as his investment was concerned he had suffered a loss of $50,000. In all fairness he should not pay any tax because he is no further ahead. He has paid the capital gains tax and has suffered a non-taxable $50,000 loss, therefore he ends up even. Another farmer with the same experience but in the reverse order, having suffered a $50,000 capital loss and later made a $50,000 capital gain would not pay any tax because the legislation provides that a loss can be carried forward indefinitely. This does not seem to be an equitable situation and the legislation should be revised to provide the same treatment in both cases.
My information is that one of our large wheat pools is among the few organizations which has supported this tax reform on the assumption that because farmers represent a low-income group with higher exemptions, many farmers will not pay tax. This is a very foolish way to judge the legislation. We should be making an effort to put farmers in a taxable position.
It has been suggested that the capital gains tax will hit farmers and small businessmen particularly hard because most of them, as we all know, endeavour to retire on the proceeds from the sale of their farms or businesses built up over a lifetime of hard work, and without high living. Now they are being put in a position where the proceeds from all this hard work will be whittled away by capital gains tax. It is suggested that farmers and small businessmen should have a registered retirement plan, the premiums of which should be deducted from the proceeds. We know there is in existence a registered retirement plan, but a sensible solution to the difficulty would be for the government to allow, through this tax legislation, the retired farmer or businessman to sell his assets and invest in the retirement plan before any capital gains tax is charged.
I should also like to refer to the treatment of co-operatives and credit unions under this legislation. These movements have been formed by people getting together for many reasons, one of which is to continue operations when things are difficult. Under the present income tax laws, co-operatives are exempt from tax for the first three years. That advantage will be wiped out as a result of this legislation. We can only assume we will see few, if any, new co-operatives. I do not think this will be good for Canada.
Under this legislation consumer dividends will remain exempt as long as they are distributed. Patronage dividends on production goods can be considered as exempt, but the goods must be taken in as income by the recipient and are taxable at the recipient's personal rate. Patronage dividends for production goods will remain as income under this bill. The capital principle has been drastically changed. At present, co-operatives cannot reduce their taxable income below 3 per cent, but the formula for calculating the tax under the bill we are discussing will include essentially every equity, such as shares, loans to members and general reserves, and the rate has been increased to 5 per cent from 3 per cent. This creates a tremendous hardship for co-operatives.
The only deduction allowed will be the interest paid on loans to members. These changes will have an accumulative effect on loans and co-operative earnings in that the earnings will have to be distributed as patronage dividends on purchases made by members of co-operatives. This means that the earnings of the co-operatives will gradually have to be distributed on the basis of the equity owned by the members. It would force them into a pattern of investor-owned corporations rather than the service corporation which they were initially established to be.
When co-operatives reach the point that this legislation forces upon them, their value as co-ops will be gone. I trust amendments will be made and presented to the government to try to alleviate this situation. When this

October 12, 1971

situation is reached, if it comes, it would be better for co-ops to incorporate as ordinary corporations. It is hard for me to believe that the government really understands what it is trying to do or what the legislation will do, and I hope the government will find some reason to reverse its stand in this regard.
One thing which I think the government should keep in mind at all times with regard to co-operatives is that any dividends paid to the private members of the co-ops are taxed at the regular personal income tax rate, the same as any other dividend. This, in my opinion, together with other taxes that co-ops pay, should be all that the government should try to get from these bodies which are basically service organizations to groups which are usually farming communities. However, now they have appeared in urban centres and they provide many services to citizens of Canada. On occasion the minister has indicated that he may see fit to make some changes in this regard.
I should like to suggest that the same consideration should be given to credit unions. Credit unions are small organizations of groups of people in a town. They could be church groups or any other group, but they come together primarily to provide a service to each other. Basically they come into existence because people have not been able to receive the services they require from banks in the community. This legislation will hit them very hard, and we hope the minister will see fit to make changes in this regard.
Credit unions have advised me that they do not require permanent capital to conduct their operations. They make loans only to the extent that members can borrow. This is regulated by federal legislation at present and they have only members' savings available to lend. They exist only to promote the economic and social interests of their members, individuals united under a common bond. Although they are chartered as legal entities and exist as incorporated companies, they have no incentives and no independent economic goals other than the welfare of their members. There is no need, then, to accumulate earnings in the credit union, and traditionally these have been allocated to members.
Again I would mention that the allocation of any of these earnings by credit unions to members would be taxed on the regular personal basis. I cannot understand why any government would feel the need to create such hardship for credit unions, thus preventing their being useful to their members, because any advantage that would be gained from borrowing or from putting savings into the credit union would be completely wiped out. They have in the past served a very useful purpose in our country and I hope will do so in the future if the opposition can get their ideas through to the government so it will make some changes.
I should like to read a letter which credit unions received from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau):
On the occasion of International Credit Union Day, I am very pleased to send my greetings to credit union members in Canada and throughout the world.
Credit unions have experienced enormous success because they encourage both regular savings and the wise use of credit. But even more important, credit unionism encourages self-help, mutual assistance, and personal involvement. In this sense credit unions are more than financial institutions, they are a positive social force within our communities.
Income Tax Act
To over 38 million members of the credit union movement in many countries of the world, I send my best wishes for continued growth and prosperity.
I cannot believe that after sending such a letter to the credit unions the Prime Minister would wish to turn around and force through the House, by his majority, legislation which would practically put credit unions out of business. I trust that amendments will be forthcoming at the committee stage and that the government will accept those which will alleviate the hardship imposed on credit unions and co-operatives through this legislation, so they may continue to serve their members as they have for many years.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few days ago the Canadian Parliament passed Bill C-262, an Act providing that the government would pay out $80,000,000 to counteract the effects of the 10 per cent American surcharge on imports from this country, and support employment in Canada.
Now as the problem today is to tax Canadians more heavily, there is before the House a legislation which is altogether different, namely Bill C-259, entitled "An Act to amend the Income Tax Act and to make certain provisions and alterations in the statute law related to or consequential upon the amendments to that Act."
This document contains 710 pages. Indeed, it is the bulkiest ever introduced in this House. Those hon. members who have been sitting here since 1965 will be able to boast of having seen everything and of having been through the mill.
In 1958, we examined Bill C-150, recognized as an omnibus bill, about 1-1/4 inch thick, which gave the green light to a very particular group of individuals. Now we are faced with a 3 inch thick bill bringing certain changes to the Income Tax Act.
After passing a bill favouring certain abnormal Canadians, the government is now ready to pass a bill introducing some changes into the Income Tax Act, namely favouring the messing around with money taken from the pocketbook of normal Canadians.
To maintain the employment level, the government, by presenting an 8 page bill, intends to pay out $80 million in grants. At the same time, it proposes, through a 710 page bill, to tax Canadians more. If an 8 page bill yields $80 million in grants, how many billions could the government collect with a 710 page bill?

October 12, 1971
Income Tax Act
Members who have spoken before me have tactfully stated that the bill now under study is confusing but in my mind it is not confusing at all as it is clear that it is simply a bill to collect more money from Canadians.
The way the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) introduces this bill astonishes me. When he accepted the post of Minister of Finance, we thought for a minute that this Canadian would assert himself; but his actions prove the contrary. In introducing this bill to us, he simply proves that he bows to another power.
On August 26 last, at the Royal York Hotel in Toronto, the hon. minister said, and I quote:
As I said in my speech on the budget, the publication of the white paper was an important step in the evolution of participatory democracy in Canada. Thanks to the ensuing debate and discussions, it has been possible to develop a program of tax reform which, in addition to meeting the needs of Canada, also reflects the views of Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, if we merely refer to that quotation, the bill now under consideration owes its birth to participatory democracy, debate and discussion. According to the minister's statement, this bill reflects the views of Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, I challenge the minister to disclose the contents of most letters which he has received. As for mine, they are available. The earliest goes back to last year at the time when the minister tabled his white paper on tax reform. I still receive some every week and I faithfully keep them.
My constituency is made up of 27,000 families, according to a report published by the Post Office Department in September last. The population of Portneuf is higher than that of Prince Edward Island and I have not yet received a single letter asking me to support the bill of the Minister of Finance.
It is obvious that for the Minister of Finance the needs of Canada are identified with those of big business. For the Minister of Finance, this reform is merely one which reflects the views of his friends who contribute to the electoral fund.
Mr. Speaker, I am still waiting for a letter urging me to support Bill C-259, and I say again that in all those that I had, the reverse is asked as regards the reforms proposed by this present Liberal government. Further to letters from ordinary citizens, I have received some from presidents of industries. The majority of firm directors have never been so concerned with public life, because they feel involved with Bill C-259. They are aware of the fact that 50 per cent of them will have to close shop if the bill passes.
This famous bill could be adopted; so there is reason for concern and that is why Canadian industrialists are worried at the present time. Their letters to us are evidence of this. Whether those industrialists live in the Montreal region, in Portneuf, in Riviere-a-Pierre, in Saint-Ray-mond, in Pont-Rouge, in l'Ancienne Lorette or Loretteville does not make much difference, the effects of this 710 page bill will be the same.
The Canadian Chamber of Commerce attempted to stop the government from taking this action through a well prepared brief sent to us on April 16, 1970.

Among the correspondence that I have received since then about Bill C-259, there is a wire sent by Mr. Andre Martel, president of the Societe Cooperative Agricole de Sainte-Catherine. I have in hand two other telegrams, one sent to me by Mr. Franpois Racette, president of the Meunerie cooperative agricole de Saint-Augustin de Portneuf, and the other by Mr. Jean-Paul Julien, president of the Cooperative agricole de Pont-Rouge.
I personally met with other managers, especially with the manager of Les Ecureuils Co-operative.
All these came as a result of the action taken by the executive director of the Cooperative Federee de Quebec, as evidenced by a letter dated August 19, which I will take the liberty to quote:

concerning Bill C-259.

Thanking you in advance, I remain
Faithfully yours,
Geo. -E Turcotte
General manager
Mr. Speaker, having been director of a co-operative for ten years, and having participated in the various activities connected with this function, I can say that in the province of Quebec alone, there are now more than 300 farm co-operatives affiliated to the Cooperative Federee. Some consumer co-operatives belong to another chain, that is the Federation des magasins co-op. According to official statistics published in the report on "Cooperation in Canada in 1969", 1,690,000 citizens of this country were distributed among 2,373 co-operatives. In view of the fact that Social Credit members are not alone in Parliament, I presume that hon. members from other parties, including even Liberals, have received the same kind of correspondence as we have. I am under the impression that they intend to rise and give us their views and those of their co-operatives in respect of the income tax reform bill.
I have received a letter from the Rural Economic Council, Portneuf Chapter. It comes from Donnacona and reads as follows:
Mr. Roland Godin, MP House of Commons,
Ottawa.
Sir:
The Rural Economic Council, Portneuf Chapter, is strongly opposed to the changes introduced in section 135 of the Income Tax Act as suggested by Bill C-259.
We think that there is no other example in the world of the concept of capital employed being applied in any tax system.
It will be impossible for the co-operatives to raise the funds necessary to reimburse capital and pay dividends with the new provisions of Section 135. It is obvious that if our co-operatives must hand out more capital than they receive, they will be forced out of business within a few years.
Income Tax Act
This method of taxation is thus anti-social and backwards: since it does not take into account the effect that a durable economic and social revival can only be achieved throughthe people. In view of those principles and their effects on the population as a whole, we believe that co-operation isthe most valuable factor of this awareness of the population.
This is why the Rural Economic Council, Portneuf Chapter, of strongly supports the views of the Conseil Canadien de la Cooperation and the Co-operative Union of Canada as they were submitted on August 11 of this year.
Yours truly,
Jean-Paul Julien, President.
Mr. Speaker, I have here the brief mentioned in that letter which is in fact the brief submitted by the Conseil Canadien de la Cooperation, a 14-page brief that concludes by asking for a meeting between the directors of the co-operative movement and the Minister of Finance to make known their objections to this bill and discuss the suggestions submitted in the brief.
I have also with me a letter addressed to all members of Parliament by Le Conseil de la Cooperation du Quebec. This letter, dated September 20, was addressed to us by Le Conseil de la Cooperation on behalf of the 21 Quebec federations which operate in all our social sectors. Among these federations is La Federation des Caisses Populaires Desjardins which has addressed a two-page letter in both official languages to all Members of Parliament. This letter was received on September 24 or 25. It reads as follows, and I quote:
Gentlemen:
Most of you are members of a Credit Union or Caisse populaire. If you are not you know certainly people from your district who are members. Almost a quarter of all Canadians are members of a Caisse populaire or Credit Union.
Bill C-259 is seeking to alter the present tax structure that applies to Caisses populaires and Credit Unions and to eliminate the exemptions they enjoy in practice. The members of the Credit Unions and Caisses populaires do not oppose taxation in itself and agree to pay their share of public expenditures. However, they wish to point out the serious concerns they feel as to the tax rates which shall be applied to the Caisses populaires and Credit Unions. They want to be sure you will keep in mind their concerns-
In connection with the main concerns of the members of the Caisses populaires, the letter stated and I quote:
I. The members of the Credit Unions and Caisses populaires are asking for a tax system equivalent to that granted to private corporations which are allowed a reduced tax rate of 25 p. 100. In effect, private corporations can almost indefinitely claim a reduced tax rate through the payment of equity dividends. Now, the provincial legislation applicable to the Caisses populaires and Credit Unions forbids them from distributing their accumulated reserves to their members thus allowing them to benefit indefinitely from the reduced tax rate.
The credit unions and the caisses populaires request that the rules be changed in order to extend the period during which the reduced rate of taxation of 25 per cent applies to them and ensure them the same situation as private companies.
Mr. Speaker, the caisses populaires, the credit unions went further, since they submitted a brief to the Minister of Finance. That brief was published on August 27 in the newspaper Ensemble. This is quite a comprehensive document from which the Canadian government could draw serious and essential amendments conducive to honest administration.

October 12, 1971
Income Tax Act
On the one hand, the present government enacts legislation designed to protect the consumers and, on the other hand, it enacts other legislation aimed at exterminating the associations made up of the same consumers, since those acts tend to the establishment of unfair and arbitrary taxation. In my opinion, we have there an instance of flagrant contradiction.
Everything established in this country under the cooperative system really represents the only wealth of the Canadian people since they are the owners and such undertakings cannot be sold to foreigners. Moreover, the co-operative formula is very simple, and within everybody's comprehension. It enables people to get information, to be protected against certain abuses and to derive profits according to their participation. Its application unfortunately was always difficult because high finance always disliked it since it wished to keep control over economic activities.
The federal government, that acted until now under pressures exerted by big corporations, has always maintained certain restrictions on the administration of financial activities of the caisses populaires and consumer co-ops.
Thus now, for instance, owing to their low assets and their non-profit feature, consumer co-operatives are dangerously threatened by Bill C-259. If that legislation is enacted, the expansion plans of the Federation of Co-op Stores to establish sales outlets in urban shopping centres will become very difficult since local co-operatives will no longer be entitled to take part in those plans.
On January 13, 1969, newspapers reported a statement made the day before in England by the right hon. Prime Minister to the effect that, in his opinion, the best way to administer a country was the communist way.
On January 21 last, I showed in the House with evidence in hand that the American communist party was infiltrating into Canada, owing to the support of certain people whose names are on the pay list of some Crown corporations.
Newspapers published recently a statement made by Mr. George Wallace, the Governor of Alabama which was reproduced in La Presse of September 27, 1971 and which reads as follows:
Scrutinizing public opinion before an eventual campain for the Presidency, Mr. Wallace-
-stated, and I quote:
"We have a crypto-communist Prime Minister in Canada, just north of our border. His background is even worse than that of President Castro himself."
Mr. Speaker, we know some liberal Members admit all this privately, and they are concerned about the fact that their chief is leading us on slippery ground.
As the Liberal Party was constituted and maintained for the defence of capitalism it is nevertheless normal for true Liberals to be concerned today about the project of their leader who can no longer hide his cards.
Mr. Speaker, it is evident that co-ops are barrier for those who wish to install communism. In socialist countries, private enterprise is a thing of the past. Since the co-operative movement has been and still is the complement of private undertaking in our country, this probably explains the action of this government, led by the right

hon. member for Mount Royal who finally made it to Prime Minister. We see his mischievious smile and with this smile he is now leading his entourage.
Mr. Speaker, the way the Minister of Finance is acting also leads us to feel that Canadians can no longer bank on him. The proof of it is that he is not even here tonight. In spite of that, I come to the conclusion that all is not lost. That the Minister of Finance should be useless, that the Prime Minister, with the co-operation of irresponsible civil servants, should prepare as barbaric a bill as Bill C-259, all that is "small potatoes" since we still have rights in this Parliament. We have the right to speak up, and the right to vote. As for voting, majority wins. This means that a bill proposed by well paid civil servants, unknown and unseen, who work according to the wishes of the Prime Minister, can be without effect unless hon. members approve it.
The Prime Minister, Mr. Trudeau, will not be the only one to support Bill C-259. It is not even necessary, because the few members of the cabinet working with him are well-known and are pursuing the same aim, that is, to abolish a system which has been tested abroad, with the results we know. However, we realize that among the members and the ministers, there are only a few who hold such views.
I therefore hope that the bill will be defeated, because I think that most will give up prostituting themselves further.
This is how I see things. I am not desperate, because I still believe that there is still a majority of honest Liberals in this House.

speechtext:
However, I think there is value in placing on the record in more or less tabular form the main changes that people like me think ought to be made to Bill C-259. Accordingly, it is not my purpose to roam around in the upper atmosphere of economic and fiscal policies. These questions are important, but they have been dealt with very well by others who have taken part in the debate.
I do not even intend to take time documenting our contention that this bill is not a piece of major tax reform but simply a number of changes in the present tax law. Rather, as I have already indicated, I wish to summarize six areas in the bill where I think very significant and important changes should be made. Indeed, it is because of the bill's shortcomings in these six areas, either that it does not go far enough or that it goes too far, that I think it should not be put over on the Canadian people at this time.
The first of these areas has to do with the income tax exemption levels. As everyone knows-and it has been repeated many times during the course of this debate-all that this bill is doing in that area is raise the income tax
October 12, 1971

exemption level for a single person from $1,000 to $1,500, and for a married taxpayer from $2,000 to $2,850.
When one considers that the present levels of $1,000 and $2,000 were established in 1949, 22 years ago, and when one also considers the increase that has taken place in the cost of living in that 22-year period, I suggest it is a delusion and a hoax on the Canadian people for the government to raise these exemption levels by only the figures that are set out in this bill. As a low, rock bottom minimum, those figures ought now to be $2,000 a year for a single person and $4,000 a year for a married person. It would even be better if they were $2,500 for a single person and $5,000 for a married person.
When one realizes that it has taken 22 years to get before the House a government proposal to raise the levels that have been in effect all this time, one can only ask, how much longer will it take to get another change? Will it be another 22 years for another few hundred dollars? By that time the whole meaning of exemption levels will have completely disappeared. It would be almost better for nothing to be done at all, and thus for the issue to be regarded as yet unresolved rather than hand the Canadian people these very low exemption levels.
Surely the whole concept of exemption levels is that there is a certain amount of money that people must have to get by, which should not be taxable. I contend, as have many members during the course of this debate, that that amount is much greater than $1,500 for single persons and $2,850 for married persons. This, Mr. Speaker, is one of the major deficiencies of Bill C-259. The fact that the government is going this far is one of the major hoaxes in this piece of legislation. I hope when we get into committee of the whole and reach the appropriate clauses that the government will pay some heed to the arguments that have been made and raise these exemptions to substantially higher levels.
The second area in which I feel this bill is deficient has to do with the amount that is allowed to workers for their expenses on the job. To put in a figure with a limit of $150 a year is an insult. Why bother with such a small allowance? For the average worker who has expenses that he can charge under this heading, his income bracket is lower than that of the wealthy; therefore, the amount that he will actually save in income tax will only be a percentage, whether it is 20 or 30 per cent, of the $150. For the wealthy, it is another little handout, a much larger one in relative terms yet meaningless to them. Those who are in the income brackets such that their tax rates are 40 or 50 per cent will get that much more off their income tax because of this $150 allowance.
I urge two things about this allowance to workers for their expenses for income tax purposes. In the first place, the amount should be higher. In the second place, this is one of many areas where the government should be introducing the concept of tax credits rather than the concept of a specified exemption. The wealthy do not need this concession, but those who earn wages in industry, the people for whom this measure supposedly has been designed, need far more than the $20 or $30 tax relief they may get out of it. They need a credit against their actual income tax for what they have to pay out for expenses incurred in connection with their work. In fact, even more important than the amount that is allowed as an exemp-
Income Tax Act
tion to workers is the need to move into this other approach, namely, the approach of allowing a tax credit instead of special exemptions as proposed in this legislation.
For many years members of this House, particularly members of this party, have been arguing for special consideration in respect of expenses that workers incur. I suppose we should be dancing with joy because at long last this principle is being recognized. But I assure you, Mr. Speaker, there is no such dancing, because the $150 is far too low for the average worker and because in principle it is wrong to do it this way rather than by way of a tax credit. We give tax credits to people who draw dividends and make profits in certain ways, but we seem to forget that approach to the problem when we get to the situation facing our workers.
My third area of criticism has to do with senior citizens. We welcome, of course, the improvements in the tax bill affecting pensioners. There are two main improvements. On the one hand we have the extra allowance for age made universal at age 65, and this allowance is to be raised to $650 per year from the present figure of $500. The other change affecting older people is the decision to regard income received under the guaranteed income supplement as non-taxable.
With respect to the latter, the government has agreed to make it effective January 1, 1971, and this will take care of a number of anomalies. It will solve the sort of problem that veterans under war veterans allowance face; their tax position has been worsened because they were pushed from war veterans allowance over to the guaranteed income supplement. Therefore, we welcome this change. However, if it was possible to make this kind of change that is designed to improve the position of older people effective as of January 1, 1971, why was it not possible to do the same thing with respect to increased exemptions for senior citizens generally? I would urge that such a change be made.
I realize that when we first started asking the minister to make that change retroactive to January 1, 1971, there were still five or six months left in the present calendar year and in a sense there seemed to be more point to it then than there now seems to be, when the end of the year is but 11 or 12 weeks away. But I would point out that the time when people are most conscious of the total amount they have to pay by way of income tax is when they file their returns in April. Unless the government makes this kind of change, it will mean that in April, 1972, when people aged 65 years or over are filing their income tax returns they will be hit between the eyes with the fact that the change that has been made-namely, the $650 exemption at age 65-is not for them until they make out their tax return a year later, in 1973. If there is this concern for the position of our older people which the government has said prompted it to make this change, I would urge that the change be made effective January 1, 1971, along with the change making the guaranteed income supplement non-taxable.
Having made those comments under the heading of what the bill does or fails to do for our older people, I want to urge that much more serious consideration be

October 12, 1971
Income Tax Act
given to the whole concept of tax credits rather than special exemptions. Just as I argued for this in the case of workers' expenses, so I argue very strongly for it in the case of our elderly and retired people. We welcome the $650 exemption and we welcome its being made universal at age 65. But there are people, not many but some, in that age bracket whose incomes are higher and this change will simply mean that of the $960 that they get as old age security, $650 will be tax free. We have to give this to the wealthy in order to get the principle established for those in the middle and lower income brackets.
I suggest that what we really ought to do is look at the literature that the organization known as Pensioners Concerned has put out and at the literature published by other organizations, and to realize the validity of their claim that retired people should not have to pay any income tax at all if their income does not exceed a certain figure. I think there is good reason and logic to accept the levels suggested by the Pensioners Concerned, which I believe are $3,000 or $3,500 for a single person and $5,000 for a married couple.
I am not suggesting that the income tax exemption levels be raised to those figures for all people 65 years of age and over, because this would give a tremendous bonanza to those in the upper income bracket. But I am saying that retired people whose income is not over $3,500 if they are single, or, if they are married, not over $5,000, should not have to pay income tax at all. The way to cope with this problem is not to fiddle around with the exemption levels, but to make the principle of tax credits applicable in their case. This is the only fair solution to this problem of how to establish exemptions and at the same time establish justice. I think in this area, as in the area of workers' expenses, the concept of tax credits ought to be considered at this time.
I strongly urge that this suggestion be looked upon, not just as an academic exercise that may produce results the next time there is a Carter report, the next time there is a white paper or another round of this sort of thing, because that may be 15 to 20 years away; I think that when we go into committee of the whole on this bill is the time to introduce this concept of tax credits.
In particular I urge, if I may now speak to the second and third points to which I have made reference, that with respect to the allowance to workers for expenses on the job, and with respect to the tax position of senior citizens or retired persons, that we adopt the tax credit principle. In terms of actual dollars, the amount that workers get as a tax credit should bear some reasonable relationship to the expenses they actually incur. In the case of retired people I think that the figures I have already quoted are reasonable.
I urge, as the retired people have urged, that having spent their lives helping to build up this country and having paid taxes, municipal provincial and federal, for decades on end, it would be little enough for a country like Canada to provide for these people in their retirement years a tax credit system that leaves them with the levels of income I have suggested. This, of course, would have to be complemented by pretty substantial increases in old age security-but that is another subject, not covered under this bill. But whatever is the bill that is before us, we must do a great deal more to provide security, justice
[Mr. Knowles (Winnipeg North Centrel.J
and dignity for our older people than we have done so far. As far as this bill is concerned, I think that in terms of taxation we can do something for this particular segment of society. I therefore hope the points I have been making will receive serious consideration when we move into committee of the whole.
I move on to my fourth point which relates to the government's intention, as set out in Bill C-259, to abolish the federal estate tax. As members of my party have pointed out on many occasions, we think this is totally wrong. We think it is wrong because it will probably lead to an estate tax war among the provinces. Even apart from that, we think the whole notion that in a society as inequitable and unjust as ours it should be possible for people to pass on great wealth to those who come after them without those who come after having to do anything about it, is completely wrong. We are completely opposed to the proposal in this bill to abolish the estate tax and we hope reconsideration will be given to that matter when we get to that portion of the bill in committee of the whole.
The fifth point I want to make is that although we welcome the decision to introduce the idea of a capital gains tax into our legislation, we think the terms of that tax as set out in the bill are not in keeping with the just society, if that idea is still around, and are not in keeping with the principles of fairness. Everywhere else the ordinary people of the country have to pay taxes on their income on the principle that a dollar is a dollar. When it comes to capital gain, of course, the government has gone soft and suggests the tax will be on only half the dollars one gains in that way. We think this is wrong and that if the principle of a capital gains tax is to be written into our legislation, it should be written in on a proper basis.
My sixth and last heading has to do, again, with something which has been a theme of a great many of the speeches made during this debate, namely, the unfairness of the government in the tax proposals it has set forth regarding co-operatives and credit unions. It has been a delight to some of us to hear many members speak about this, particularly those from the government side of the House. The case has been well made and I do not intend to repeat it in terms of details or argument, but I do urge the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) and the government to realize how strong is the feeling about this matter among the many hundreds of thousands of Canadians who are members of co-operatives and credit unions. The clauses of the bill which deal with this matter are quite offensive to many Canadians and I hope that when we get to these clauses something will be done about them.

FINANCE-GOVERNMENT POSITION RESPECTING NEGATIVE INCOME TAX FORMULA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 16, 1971, I put a question to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) regarding some tax injustice, more precisely in order to find out, and I quote:
-whether he approves the negative tax formula suggested by many authorities as a method to assure a better distribution of the purchasing power? Does the minister believe that it would be a desirable means to stimulate the economy?
The Chair then stated that my question invited the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) or the Minister of Finance to give an opinion, and so we did not hear the view of the minister. So, I invite him tonight to tell the public what he thinks of that.
The negative tax is a return which would benefit those who earn less than $3,000 annually.
Mr. Speaker, we all know of course that a tax policy is required to serve first the interests of Canadians and to provide each individual with a vital minimum, as a birthright.
I think it is a reversal of the roles that is needed. It is merely a question of distribution; we should distribut the surplus of our national product, which was of $91 billion in 1971, while consumption was only of $50 billion, which gives a difference of $41 billion.
So, we must give back to the country its national balance and its economic independence. The whole world is asking for economic balance and not equality. Revolutionary experiences carried out in the name of equality have all failed.
Mr. Speaker, there is no economic future with the present system. It is our whole way of thinking that must be changed, so that our governments will not remain deaf to the representations of the people who tell us again and again that what they need is food, clothing, housing and education.
Would a negative tax provide the essential and take these factors into account? I doubt it. But I must admit that it would bring a degree of relief to the poorer classes.

Above all, it would be a recognition of the importance of a number of human beings.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that we should analyze the causes of all these difficulties which are, after all, only administrative and economic problems which call for the use of the mental faculties of the ruling class.
Mr. Speaker, every individual lives within his family and within society. Everyone does something for choice or for profit. I would say that on the one hand, there is love and on the other, interest. Let us stop believing that the two are necessarily opposed. There must be a way of reconciling one with the other.
Parliament consists of 264 members elected by the citizens of Canada under the Canada Elections Act. It is the responsibility of members to see that justice prevail in 1971 among the 22 million Canadians, according to the production of goods and services in that year.
It may be normal, when exercising supreme authority, that governments are inclined, with equal opportunities, to favour their friends, their constituents or members of their political party, but without prejudice of their love for other Canadians. Interest should not do away with love!
If the Prime Minister has any feelings for the 22 million Canadians who are subjected to the "supreme" authority he shares with the other 29 ministers and the 264 members, he will no doubt see to it that the monetary, economic and political mechanisms bring about a fair distribution of goods and services among these 22 million citizens, according to their essential needs, before someone piles up too large a share of this tremendous production, after having spent what he needed to live in affluence and not in luxury. That is simple and understandable!
If Parliament had the social attitude it should have, capital would automatically become social as well as labour. Credit would automatically become social in all its institutions, in every Canadian family.
The Canadian government makes sure every month that the 22 million citizens are well administered according to the national production, according to the administrative formula recognized by all managers: The revenue is equal to expenses and net profits.
Every Canadian must get a sufficient guaranteed income to provide for his essential expenses, and to allow for a certain margin for savings, profit and contingencies, according to the formula recognized by all-
