maintopic: AGRICULTURE-POTATOES-ASSURANCE TO PRODUCERS RESPECTING SEED EXPORT MARKET
AGRICULTURE-POTATOES-ASSURANCE TO PRODUCERS RESPECTING SEED EXPORT MARKET
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise this evening to deal again with a matter of great importance to the potato producers of this country but primarily, I think, to the seed producers of Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. As is well known, many aspects of agriculture in this country have been severely affected by two recent economic decisions, one taken by this country and one taken by the U.S.
The first was the effect of the floating of the dollar, which had a very serious effect on our agricultural exports to the United States and in effect decreased the competitive advantage that our potatoes and other agricultural products enjoyed in the U.S. Then, of course, more recently we were faced with the imposition of the 10 per cent surtax which has created a very serious problem, as has been acknowledged on a number of occasions by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) in this House, beginning the first week of the reconvened session in early September and as late as this afternoon when the minister made reference to the special attention that was being given to the turkey producers of Canada.
I think that many members of this House, and certainly many thousands of potato growers, have been most unsatisfied with the answers given to date by the Minister of Agriculture with respect to what forms of assistance might be forthcoming for those faced with very serious prohibitions on the entry of their products to the U.S. and the amount of return they could expect for that product. The hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. MacLean), myself, the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) and others have attempted from time to time to obtain a specific answer from the Minister of Agriculture with respect to what forms of assistance will be forthcoming.
The minister has talked in general terms about the agricultural stabilization board, suggesting that under the act assistance would be forthcoming. There have been at least two meetings of which I am aware with the departmental officials and with the ministers of agriculture of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, but no clear statement has yet been brought forth as to the nature of the assistance that will be provided. The minister has indicated that at the appropriate time he will make a statement indicating what assistance will be available in a more specific way, and yet assistance is required almost immediately.
We know that the potato harvest in New Brunswick is almost completed. The potato harvest in Prince Edward Island is more than half way completed. Our harvest comes a little later because of a later frost period and I am informed by the potato shippers in P.E.I. that we have already loaded ships for export, that other ships are being loaded at present and these are primarily destined for U.S. markets. I am also informed that if we do not have an indication within the next week or so of the kind of assistance that the minister will bring forward, markets will be closed off for hundreds of thousands of hundredweights of potatoes that we would normally ship into the seed importing areas of Florida, Puerto Rico and the New England states.
It is a well known fact that most potato producers produce at least 15 per cent to 20 per cent above and beyond that which they can hold in their potato-holding facilities. In other words, these are potatoes that must clear the market before the heavy frost sets in in the middle or late November. Therefore, if potato producers do not have the luxury of holding their product for an indefinite period of time, as might be done with other kinds of produce, they are forced on to market and they must have an assurance immediately as to the kind of assistance that might be provided.
I should like to mention (wo things that might be taken into consideration. One is tne possibility of freight assistance or subsidy that might enable new export markets to be opened up as an alternative to the present U.S. ones which are becoming increasingly difficult for us. I realize that we would have to take into account the necessity of facing certain areas where there might be retaliation through increased tariffs, but I think certainly the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Department of Agriculture should be examining the proposal.
Second, if in the employment support bill we have adopted the principle of two-thirds reimbursement for industries directly affected by the Nixon surtax, the same principle could apply to agriculture, namely, a two-thirds reimbursement could at least be given as assistance in direct wages to those involved at the point of assembly, to those involved with stevedoring and the assembling of potato shipments for export. The nature of that program would not open up retaliatory measures on the part of the U.S. and would ensure that the present producers, growers, distributors and shippers would not be adversely affected or be in very great danger of losing their markets entirely.
I trust that the Minister of Agriculture or his representative can give some clear assurance this evening that action of this or a similar nature will be taken within the next few days so that the already serious situation of our potato growers will not be worsened.

maintopic: AIR TRANSPORT-ESTABLISHMENT OF NORDAIR AS REGIONAL CARRIER FOR NORTHEASTERN ONTARIO AND NORTHWESTERN QUEBEC-ONTARIO APPLICATION FOR REGIONAL CHARTER
AIR TRANSPORT-ESTABLISHMENT OF NORDAIR AS REGIONAL CARRIER FOR NORTHEASTERN ONTARIO AND NORTHWESTERN QUEBEC-ONTARIO APPLICATION FOR REGIONAL CHARTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on September 29, as recorded at page 8278 of Hansard, I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) the following question:
Under our national air policy as it involves regional carriers, have negotiations been finalized regarding Nordair as the regional carrier for northeastern Ontario and northwestern Quebec?
The minister replied:
Not that I know of, Mr. Speaker. There have been discussions between Air Canada and Nordair with respect to possible exchange or co-operation for certain air routes but to the moment at least, and so far as I know, no conclusions have been reached.
I then asked:
Has a charter been sought from the Canadian Transport Commission by the Ontario government through its commercial carrier, White River Air Service? If so, what role in the regional transportation system is being filled by this application?
The reason I asked this question, Mr. Speaker, is that in northern Ontario we are being told that Air Canada will not be able to service both the area of northeastern Ontario and northwestern Quebec for the very simple reason that it has not any planes on order that will operate economically in that area. The applications that have been made have both been approved by the Air Transport Committee of the Canadian Transport Commission. They were made on September 30 and were in regard to Voya-geur Airways Limited and White River Air Services, operating under the name of norOntair.
The Ontario government has got into the regional air service and is operating a circular route that starts in Timmins, or Sault Ste Marie, and covers the towns of Sault Ste Marie, Timmins, Earlton and Sudbury, returning to Sault Ste Marie. This has since been changed and the flights will originate in Sudbury. This airline is operating two aircraft owned by the Ontario government and leased for the sum of $1, and obviously it is going to play a role in the regional air service.

The Voyageur application, Mr. Speaker, is from Ottawa to North Bay and return, and also is going to play a role. But these two services that are operating in the region do not make any connection with each other, and while it is possible to get on the airline in Earlton and go to Sudbury, if you are coming to Ottawa it is necessary to get from Sudbury to North Bay to make a connection with the other airline. This is the whole problem and it is the problem the Minister of Transport outlined on October 20, 1966, and again on August 15, 1969, when he said that in this case the organization of regional service in the area might require the consideration of route service between North Bay and Ottawa and consequently have an effect on the viability'of the service authorized by this decision.
We in northern Ontario, Mr. Speaker, are not interested in getting on an airplane and going around in a circle. We want to get on an airplane at any point in northern Ontario and make connection with the national service in Canada, that is Air Canada, with its lines running east and west, or Canadian Pacific also running east and west. Anything less is already being handled by small charter aircraft in the area. I think it involves a decision by the Minister of Transport to inform the Canadian Transport Commission as to the integration of the various services chartered by the Canadian Transport Commission, to integrate service that will provide the opportunity of travelling from one place in northern Ontario to either the major centres of Montreal, Ottawa or Toronto. Any carrier that has not a direct connection to those major points is not serving the needs of the region of northeastern Ontario nor, I presume, northwestern Quebec.
So I ask the question, Mr. Speaker, because I think it should be brought to the attention of the Minister of Transport that the people in northern Ontario are very concerned that he has not insisted that Air Canada buy a 20-passenger aircraft for this type of service. We in northern Ontario are very much in favour of Air Canada being able to continue the service that we receive and, what is more, in improving that service.
I believe that the more flights a day there are, the more passengers will travel on the airline. To run a passenger aircraft out of my area, leaving in the middle of the day and getting into Toronto or Montreal late in the afternoon does not serve the needs of businessmen. Most businessmen therefore drive. I suggest if we are to charter commercial flights within this region nothing can be served by having them go around like the Ontario government service, in a circle, making no connections with anything, and in fact just moving from my area about 12 businessmen who have an interest in travelling through northeastern Ontario and getting to all the major points.
It seems to me that the Minister of Transport in announcing regional policy has an obligation to see that the Canadian Transport Commission puts this policy into effect. While I am in agreement that they have reserved the right for Nordair to get into the area, we have a bigger obligation and that is not to ask an unknown regional carrier to take on an additional responsibility. We as a Parliament have a responsibility to insist that Air Canada buy the type of aircraft that will enable them to service the regional areas in which they now operate, and continue to do so. Anything less will be a dereliction of duty on the part of the Minister of Transport.
October 12, 1971

maintopic: AIR TRANSPORT-ESTABLISHMENT OF NORDAIR AS REGIONAL CARRIER FOR NORTHEASTERN ONTARIO AND NORTHWESTERN QUEBEC-ONTARIO APPLICATION FOR REGIONAL CHARTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the subject of negotiations between Air Canada and Nordair, and in answer to the questions asked by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) on September 29, the minister answered that discussions had reached no conclusion at that time. I must say that as far as I know, the situation is still the same and no decisions have been reached.
The hon. member also talked of his concern about the development of air service to northeastern Ontario. I am sure he has now read the decision of the Air Transport Committee of the Canadian Transport Commission on September 30. The decision was in favour of additional air service to service the points of Sudbury, Sault Ste Marie, Timmins and Earlton. The application, as he mentioned in his question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
Jamieson) was made by White River Air Services, Limited.
Briefly, the service in question was considered as an experimental service for a period of three years and there were additional limitations spelled out to the carrier to protect the public interest as well as the competitive position of other air carriers in this region. There also was direct reference to the regional air carrier policy and its application to this service. The proposed service is third level in nature and supplements the existing service in this region.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has made some interesting points which I will be glad to bring to the attention of the Minister of Transport. I will also provide the hon. member with a copy of the decision which I brought with me.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 9.34 p.m.
